1.summary: How we see colour (light, matter and the eye's rods and cones) and how colour is described: the Munsell system, CIE 1931 XYZ and xyY, CIELAB, HSV and HSL, RGB and CMY(K).

facts.gist: To see colour you need three things: light, an object and the human visual system.
facts.d: To see color you need light, an object (matter) and the human visual system.

facts.gist: Light with a wavelength of about 380–780 nm; below it is ultraviolet, above it infrared.
facts.d: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation with wavelength 380–780 nm (approx. 400–700 nm); UV below, IR above.

Light is characterized by its spectral energy distribution P(λ), the relationship between intensity and wavelength. Equal-energy white contains all visible wavelengths in correct proportions, all equally intense: E - P(λ) = const.

facts.gist: Matter transmits, reflects or absorbs light. The refractive index says how much slower light is in a material than in a vacuum.
facts.d: Matter interacts with light by transmission, reflection and absorption. Transmission is characterized by the refractive index = speed of light in vacuum / speed in material (water RI = 1.333).

Perfect mirror = specular (directional) reflection; rough surface = diffuse (matte); diffuse + specular is the most common in practice. Absorption: waves of certain wavelengths are absorbed. Optical transmittance = amount of EM radiation passing through a substance without being absorbed or scattered.

facts.gist: A few million cones see colour in good light; over 100 million rods see gray in weak light. Three cone types: blue (S), green (M), red (L).
facts.d: Cones 6–9 million (avg. 4.5 million as printed): color vision in relatively bright light. Rods 100–120 million (avg. 90 million as printed): grayscale vision at low light. Peaks: S/blue cones 420 nm, rods 498 nm, M/green cones 534 nm, L/red cones 564 nm.

facts.gist: Rods: very sensitive, slow, low acuity, one type, night. Cones: less sensitive, fast, high acuity, three types, day.
facts.d: Rods: low acuity, very high sensitivity (diffuse light), slow reaction, shapes and movement, 1 type, scotopic (night) vision, impairment causes twilight/night blindness. Cones: high acuity, low sensitivity (direct light), fast reaction, color perception, 3 types, photopic vision, impairment causes loss of color perception / sharpness.

facts.gist: Photopic = day, only cones. Mesopic = transition, colours fade. Scotopic = night, shades of gray.
facts.d: Photopic (daytime): sufficient light, ONLY the cones are involved. Mesopic: transitional phase as light decreases, partial or gradual loss of color perception. Scotopic: minimal light intensity, world seen in shades of gray.

facts.gist: As it gets dark, reds look darker than the other colours.
facts.d: Disturbance in perception of color brightness in low light: reds appear darker than other colors as light decreases. Relative sensitivity peaks: scotopic 507 nm, photopic 555 nm.

facts.gist: Nyctalopia: cannot see in dim light (night blindness). Hemeralopia: cannot see in bright light.
facts.d: Night blindness (nyctalopia) impairs or prevents vision in relatively dim light and is a symptom of an eye disorder. Hemeralopia is the opposite: inability to see in bright light.
Describing color by P(λ) is cumbersome/redundant because different spectral distributions evoke the same visual sensation. Models listed: Munsell, CIE-XYZ, RGB, CMY(K), HSV, YUV/YIQ, YCbCr, others.

facts.gist: A colour is three numbers: hue, value (lightness) and chroma (saturation).
facts.d: Albert Henry Munsell, 'A Color Notation', 1905 (idea originated with Newton). A color is given by three numbers: VALUE = lightness, CHROMA = saturation, HUE = measured hue.

facts.gist: Five primary hues (R, Y, G, B, P) and five intermediate ones on a dial.
facts.d: 5 primary hues: red (R), yellow (Y), green (G), blue (B), magenta/purple (P). 5 intermediate: YR, GY, BG, PB, RP. Arranged on a compass-like dial with labels.

facts.gist: Value runs from black (0) to white (10). Chroma is the distance from gray, and its maximum differs between hues.
facts.d: VALUE: 9 discrete gray levels 1N–9N (2N dark gray, 5N medium gray), 0N = black, 10N = white. CHROMA: difference between pure color and gray, discrete scale whose range depends on hue and value; different areas have different maximal chroma (!).

facts.t: Munsell notation and Book of Color
facts.d: Example: yellow ochre = 10YR 5/6 (hue 10YR, value 5, chroma 6); brown is not a pure hue. Perceptual difference between adjacent colors is roughly equal, so the space is shown on 100 color charts: the 'Munsell Book of Color'.

facts.gist: CIE, the International Commission on Illumination, matched colours with red, green and blue lights; three real lights cannot reproduce every colour.
facts.d: CIE = Commission Internationale de l'Éclairage. 1931 color matching with a visual colorimeter (tintometer) using adjustable primaries R 700 nm, G 546.1 nm, B 435.8 nm. Not all spectral colors can be balanced; three pure spectral colors cannot reproduce all shades.

facts.gist: CIE-RGB needs negative weights, so fictitious primaries X, Y, Z were defined; Y is luminance and nothing is negative.
facts.d: CIE-RGB matching functions need negative weights (or additional colors), so CIE-RGB is inconvenient. New fictitious XYZ primaries were defined: Y = luminance (cone sensitivity); X and Z chosen so all visible colors have non-negative components. Computing XYZ for all spectra forms a solid containing all visible colors.

facts.gist: The horseshoe chart shows chromaticity without brightness: pure spectral colours on the edge, white near the middle.
facts.d: xyY reduces 3-D XYZ to 2-D: x, y = chromaticity, Y = luminance. Cross-section by plane X+Y+Z=1 projected onto the X-Y plane = CIE-XYZ chromaticity diagram. It has NO brightness information; spectral colors on the envelope, other colors inside; white point C at (0.333, 0.333).

1) dominant wavelength (line from C through A to the envelope), 2) complementary color (line from A through C to the opposite edge), 3) addition A+B lies on segment AB, 4) color triangle R-G-B: interior holds all sums of R, G, B, 5) comparing device gamuts (sRGB, Adobe RGB 1998, ProPhoto RGB, ColorMatch RGB, SWOP CMYK, D65 white point).

facts.gist: L = lightness, a = green to red, b = blue to yellow. Device-independent, close to human perception, used to measure colour difference (ΔE).
facts.d: L = lightness (0 black, 100 reference white); a = green(-)/red(+); b = blue(-)/yellow(+). Device-independent nonlinear transformation of CIE XYZ relative to a reference white; approximately perceptually uniform. Uses: color matching/QC (ΔE), segmentation, k-means palette extraction, color management, editing L separately from a*, b*.

facts.t: HSV model and HSV vs CIELAB
facts.gist: HSV (hue, saturation, value) makes it easy to describe a colour; CIELAB is precise and device-independent.
facts.d: color = [H, S, V], H ∈ [0–360°], S, V ∈ [0, 1]; cone axis = gray axis; algorithms convert HSV to RGB and CMY. Advantage: easy, interactive description of an imagined color. HSV = intuitive for programmers/designers (saturation slider); CIE-LAB = precise, device-independent (print must match screen).
Color space is a solid of two cones; resembles perceptual models (Munsell); fully saturated colors on a circle at lightness 1/2; luminance 0 = black, 1 = white; color = Hue, Saturation, Lightness.

facts.gist: RGB adds light (monitor, starts from black); CMY subtracts light with ink (print, starts from white).
facts.d: RGB: [R,G,B] in [0,1], additive, diagonal [0,0,0]-[1,1,1] = grayscale black to white, e.g. monitor display. CMY: [C,M,Y] in [0,1], subtractive, diagonal = gray scale white to black, e.g. printing on white paper. Both: advantage = easy reproduction of a described color; disadvantage = difficult to describe an imagined color. Example: 442 nm monochromatic light = 0.77B + 0.11G + 0R.

facts.gist: Y = brightness, the other two = colour. YUV belongs to PAL, YIQ to NTSC. The eye cares more about Y, so colour can be compressed.
facts.d: Luminance Y = brightness (grayscale image); chrominance (UV, IQ) = color. YUV is the PAL system: the eye is more sensitive to luminance than chrominance, so brightness and color are separated for compression; Y errors matter more than U, V errors. YIQ is the NTSC system: I and Q are used because U, V colors do not match human perception; downward compatible with B&W TV that uses only Y.

facts.gist: The digital cousin of YUV, scaled and shifted, used in JPEG and MPEG.
facts.d: Often confused with YUV; used with JPEG/MPEG; chrominance always in [0, 1]; a scaled and shifted YUV; YUV is 'analog', YCbCr is 'digital'.

facts.gist: Y + orange + green chrominance: simple, reversible without loss, used in H.264, HEVC and JPEG XR.
facts.d: Directly related to RGB; Y + chrominance green (Cg) + chrominance orange (Co); lossless RGB conversion using fewer bits; used in H.264/MPEG-4 AVC, HEVC, JPEG XR. Advantages over YCbCr: simpler and faster calculations, better color-plane correlation (better compression), lossless reversibility.

facts.gist: The temperature of a black body with the same colour. Low K looks warm (orange), high K cold (blue); D65 = 6,500 K.
facts.d: Measure of the color rendering of a light source, in K, based on blackbody radiation of a perfect black body (which does not exist): heated, it goes dark red, yellow, white, light blue. Paradox: low K perceived as warm, high K as cold. 1,800–2,000 K candle/sunrise; 2,700–3,000 K tungsten bulb; 4,000–4,500 K office/moonlight (neutral white); 5,000–5,500 K noon sun/flash; 6,500 K slightly cloudy sky = D65 (computer graphics); 8,000–10,000 K clear blue sky in deep shadow.

formulas.name: xyY to XYZ
formulas.expr: X = Y * x / y (printed as X = Y * X/y); Z = Y * (1 - x - y) / y; x, y = chromaticity, Y = luminance measured by colorimeter

formulas.name: Tristimulus integrals
formulas.expr: X = k ∫ P(λ) x̄(λ) dλ; Y = k ∫ P(λ) ȳ(λ) dλ; Z = k ∫ P(λ) z̄(λ) dλ

formulas.name: Chromaticity plane
formulas.expr: X + Y + Z = 1 (cross-section plane, projected onto X-Y plane)

formulas.name: YUV chrominance
formulas.expr: U = B - Y; V = R - Y

formulas.name: YCoCg inverse steps
formulas.expr: Tmp = Y - Cg; R = Tmp + Co; G = Y + Cg; B = Tmp - Co

traps: Cone vs rod counts swapped: cones 6-9 million (avg 4.5 M), rods 100-120 million (avg 90 M); the printed averages lie below the ranges.
RGB diagonal runs black to white ([0,0,0] = black); CMY diagonal runs white to black ([0,0,0] = white).
YUV belongs to PAL, YIQ to NTSC; YUV is 'analog', YCbCr is 'digital' (JPEG/MPEG).
Nyctalopia = cannot see in dim light (night blindness); hemeralopia = cannot see in bright light.
Munsell CHROMA = saturation, VALUE = lightness; value levels 1N-9N with 0N black and 10N white; max chroma differs by region.
Color temperature paradox: low K looks warm (yellow/orange), high K looks cold (blue); D65 = 6,500 K.
CIE chromaticity diagram has no brightness information, but in XYZ/xyY the Y component IS luminance.
Purkinje: reds (not blues) get darker in dim light; scotopic peak 507 nm vs photopic 555 nm.
HSV is a single cone, HSL a double cone.

2.summary: From light to pixels: camera controls, CCD and CMOS sensors, colour filter arrays and sensor formats, then histograms, transforms (DFT, DCT, DWT), filtering and HDR imaging.

facts.gist: A two-dimensional array of pixel values: gray levels, colours or colour indexes.
facts.d: A digital image is a 2D array f = f(x, y), x = 0..N-1, y = 0..M-1, where N and M are image width and height. Pixel values can be a gray level in {0..S}, a colour [r g b] with r, g, b in {0..S}, or a colour index in {0..S}.

facts.gist: Lens → sensor with filter → ADC → processor → storage. Quality depends on lens, sensor and processing together.
facts.d: Pipeline: Lens → Sensor (CFA) → ADC → DSP → Storage. Image quality is jointly determined by lens, sensor and image processing engine (optics, sensor and processing).

facts.gist: Focal length: angle of view. Aperture: light and depth of field. Shutter: motion blur. ISO: gain.
facts.d: Focal length: angle of view for a given sensor size. Aperture: light reaching the sensor and depth of field. Shutter speed: exposure duration and motion blur (1 s blurs flowing water, 1/1000 s freezes it). ISO: signal gain and rendered brightness. Other features: autofocus, stabilization, viewfinder.

facts.t: Focal length vs angle of view
facts.d: Example: 20 mm lens about 94°, 50 mm about 46°, 500 mm about 5°. Shorter focal length gives a wider view.

facts.gist: Small f-number = wide aperture = shallow depth of field; f/16 = large depth of field.
facts.d: A smaller f-number means a wider aperture (scale f/2.8, f/4, f/5.6, f/8, f/11, f/16). f/2.8 gives shallow depth of field; f/16 gives large depth of field.

facts.gist: Amplifies the signal; it does not collect more light and it makes noise visible.
facts.d: ISO changes signal gain; it does not increase the light collected. Higher ISO (ISO 3200 vs ISO 200) gives more visible noise and less fine detail.

facts.gist: Charge-coupled device: light creates charge, which is shifted row by row to one output amplifier.
facts.d: CCD = charge-coupled device. Light generates charge in photosensitive pixels; charge is transferred to an output amplifier by clocked parallel shifting of rows into a serial shift register that outputs the data.

facts.gist: 1969 first CCD (Boyle and Smith, Bell Labs), 1974 first CCD used for images (Fairchild).
facts.d: 1969: W. Boyle and G. Smith (Bell Labs) designed the first CCD (data storage). 1974: Fairchild Electronics, first CCD used for image acquisition (100 × 100 px). 2015: Canon demonstrated a 250 MP CMOS sensor. 2020: SLAC captured 3,200 MP images with a CCD array.

facts.gist: CCD moves charge and gives an analog output; CMOS converts in each pixel and often gives a digital output.
facts.d: Readout: CCD charge transfer vs CMOS pixel-level conversion. Output: CCD analog voltage vs CMOS often digital. Integration: CCD more external circuitry vs CMOS often integrated. Speed: CCD architecture-dependent vs CMOS parallel readout options. Fill factor, noise, dynamic range, power/cost are design-, device- or application-dependent for both. Choose by measured performance and application requirements.

facts.gist: Filters over the pixels. Bayer: two green, one red, one blue. RGBE adds emerald; CMYY and CYGM use magenta.
facts.d: A CFA places colour filters over sensor pixels. Bayer uses two green, one red and one blue filter (G-R-G-B, most popular mosaic). Other CFAs: RGBE (red, green, blue, emerald), CMYY (cyan, magenta, yellow, yellow), CYGM (cyan, yellow, green, magenta).

Canon PowerShot G2: about 4.1 MP total, about 3.9 MP effective, 1/1.8-inch sensor, Bayer CFA, ISO 100/200/400. Kodak compact: 8.1 MP CCD, fixed lens with no optical zoom, JPEG capture, SD/SDHC storage, VGA video at 30 fps.

Full Frame 36 × 24 mm = 864 mm²; APS-H 28.2 × 18.7 = 527; APS-C (Nikon/Sony/Pentax/Fuji) about 23.6 × 15.7 = about 370; APS-C (Canon) 22.2 × 14.8 = 329; Foveon 20.7 × 13.8 = 286; Four Thirds 17.3 × 13 = 225; 1-inch 13.2 × 8.8 = 116; 2/3-inch 8.6 × 6.6 = 57; 1/1.7-inch 7.6 × 5.7 = 43; 1/2.5-inch 5.76 × 4.29 = 25. Crop factor chart: full frame 1.00, APS-H 1.29, Four Thirds 2.00, medium format 0.50.

Introduced in 1999. Uses octagonal rather than rectangular photosites, giving higher horizontal and vertical resolution (at the expense of diagonal resolution) than a traditional sensor of equal pixel count; claimed high sensitivity and dynamics, better colour reproduction, miniaturisation.

Layered sensor: blue, green and red sensors stacked vertically (blue on top, red at the bottom) using the different absorption depths of light in silicon; stack about 7 microns wide and under 5 microns deep. Bayer instead uses a filter mosaic over single-layer pixels.

facts.gist: Turns the analog signal into codes; more bits mean more levels (8 bits = 256).
facts.d: An ADC quantizes an analog signal into a digital code. An n-bit ADC provides 2^n codes: 8-bit 256, 10-bit 1,024, 12-bit 4,096 levels.

facts.gist: The camera processor does demosaicing, enhancement and compression. RAW = data without conversion.
facts.d: The in-camera DSP performs colour interpolation (demosaicing), image enhancement and colour correction, image compression and computational photography. Processing engine steps shown: RGB image production, brightness, white balance, sharpness, contrast. RAW data is recorded without conversion; TIFF has no compression; JPEG is compressed by a special LSI.

SD up to 2 GB; SDHC more than 2 GB up to 32 GB; SDXC more than 32 GB up to 2 TB; SDUC more than 2 TB up to 128 TB. Sony Memory Stick: relatively slow (< 50 MB/s), 128 MB (Original), 32 GB (PRO), 2 TB (XC). CompactFlash: Type I 43 × 36 × 3.3 mm, Type II 43 × 36 × 5 mm, 2 MB to 512 GB (CF5.0 up to 128 PB). XQD: 38.5 × 29.8 × 3.8 mm, 2 TB+, PCI Express interface, about 500 MB/s R/W.

facts.t: Canon EOS R5 Mark II vs Nikon Z8
facts.d: Price 4,299 vs 3,999 USD; 45.0 vs 45.7 MP; both full-frame stacked CMOS; native ISO 100-51,200 vs 64-25,600; raw burst 30 vs 20 fps; full-res JPEG 30 fps both; raw video 8K/60p vs 8K/60p N-Raw; 3.2-inch LCD fully articulated vs two-way tilt; CFexpress Type B + UHS-II SD both; launch July 2024 vs May 2023; DPReview 93% vs 94%. Green cells mark different specs, not a winner.

facts.gist: Pixel and logic chips bonded vertically: faster readout, less rolling-shutter distortion, but not a global shutter.
facts.d: Pixel layer (back-illuminated photodiodes) and logic layer (high-speed readout) are bonded vertically; some designs add memory. Advantages: faster readout reduces rolling-shutter distortion, rapid bursts and more frequent AF updates, high-resolution video at high frame rates. Trade-offs: more complex fabrication and bonding; dynamic range depends on design, not the label; stacked does not imply global shutter.

facts.gist: Counts how many pixels have each brightness level.
facts.d: A histogram counts pixels at each intensity level, H(i) = card{(x, y): image(x, y) = i}. Example 256 × 256 image = 65,536 pixels. Horizontal axis = brightness (dark left to bright right, shadows/midtones/highlights), vertical axis = number of pixels.

facts.gist: Pixels piled up at 255 = overexposed; piled up near 0 = underexposed.
facts.d: Highlight clipping: many pixels at level 255 indicates overexposure. Dark image: many pixels near levels 6-7 indicates underexposure.

facts.gist: Spreads the levels with the cumulative histogram; improves contrast when the levels are bunched together.
facts.d: Redistributes pixel intensities using the cumulative histogram. It can improve global contrast when intensities occupy a narrow range; the result depends on the image, so inspect detail and noise afterwards.

facts.gist: FFT: global frequencies, periodic noise. DCT: blocks, JPEG. DWT: location and scale, denoising. The FFT is just a fast DFT.
facts.d: Transforms express pixels as coefficients easier to filter, compress or analyze. FFT: global spatial frequencies with magnitude and phase; frequency filtering, periodic-noise removal; limited spatial localization. DCT: cosine patterns within blocks; JPEG compression, energy compaction; block artifacts with strong quantization. DWT: local detail at multiple scales; denoising, multiscale analysis, compression; captures location and scale. FFT is a fast algorithm for computing the DFT, not a different transform.

f(x, y) (spatial image) → F(u, v) (frequency-domain coefficients). F(u, v) contains magnitude and phase; an N × N image has N × N complex DFT coefficients; the inverse transform reconstructs the image. A constant 8 × 8 image has a single non-zero (DC) coefficient; a rectangular pulse and a photo patch show a large DC term plus smaller coefficients.

Input f(x, y) → processing algorithm → output g(x, y). Typical operations: image enhancement, geometric transformations (rotation, translation, uniform and non-uniform scaling, reflection, shearing), colour correction, segmentation of image regions, HDR imaging.

facts.gist: Gaussian: weighted average, blurs detail. Median: middle value, removes isolated spots.
facts.d: Gaussian: each pixel replaced by a weighted average of its neighbourhood, mask normalized to sum to 1 (example mask 2 4 2 / 4 8 4 / 2 4 2, sum 32); blurs fine detail. Median: the pixel and its 8 neighbours are sorted non-decreasingly and the 5th element is the output; removes isolated dark spots.

facts.gist: Combines bracketed exposures to keep shadows and highlights; one stop more = twice the light.
facts.d: HDR represents a wider range of scene brightness. Bracketed exposures (example -4, -2, +2, +4 stops) capture shadow and highlight detail. One stop more exposure doubles the light collected.

formulas.name: Pixel value types
formulas.expr: gray: f(x, y) in {0..S}; colour: f(x, y) = [r(x, y) g(x, y) b(x, y)], r, g, b in {0..S}; colour index: f(x, y) in {0..S}

formulas.name: Sensor area
formulas.expr: area = width × height (Full Frame 36 × 24 mm = 864 mm²)

formulas.name: Histogram
formulas.expr: H(i) = card{(x, y): image(x, y) = i}

formulas.name: Gaussian filter
formulas.expr: g(x, y) = (1 / sum_x sum_y m(x, y)) * sum_x sum_y m(x, y) * f(x, y); example mask m = [2 4 2; 4 8 4; 2 4 2], weight sum 32

formulas.name: Median filter
formulas.expr: g(x, y) = 5th element of the 9 values of the 3 × 3 neighbourhood of f(x, y) sorted in non-decreasing order

formulas.name: Exposure stops
formulas.expr: light ratio = 2^(difference in stops); +1 stop = 2 × light

traps: Smaller f-number = WIDER aperture and SHALLOWER depth of field (f/2.8 shallow, f/16 large), not narrower.
ISO only changes signal gain; it does not increase the light collected, and higher ISO adds visible noise.
FFT is not a separate transform; it is a fast algorithm for computing the DFT.
DCT (not FFT) is the JPEG transform; DWT (not FFT) captures both location and scale.
Bayer = two GREEN, one red, one blue (G-R-G-B); RGBE adds emerald; CMYY and CYGM contain magenta.
CCD = charge transfer with analog voltage output; CMOS = pixel-level conversion, often digital output; easy to swap.
1969 Boyle and Smith (Bell Labs) built the CCD for data storage; 1974 Fairchild made the first imaging CCD (100 × 100 px).
Stacked CMOS does not imply global shutter, and its dynamic range depends on design, not on the 'stacked' label.
A/D conversion is done by the ADC before the DSP; it is not a DSP task (DSP = demosaicing, enhancement, compression, computational photography).
One stop doubles the light, so n stops = 2^n times (8 stops = 256 times), not n times; SDHC ends at 32 GB, SDXC at 2 TB, SDUC at 128 TB.

3.summary: The history of television and how analog TV works: interlaced scanning, luminance and sync levels, colour-difference signals, gamma correction, the composite signal, channels and the NTSC, PAL and SECAM standards.

facts.gist: Greek tele (far) + Latin visio (the image seen). Phi phenomenon: Max Wertheimer, 1912.
facts.d: Television = Greek 'tele' (far) + Latin 'visio' (the image seen). The 'phi phenomenon' was described by Max Wertheimer in 1912.

facts.gist: The picture is sent line by line; the signal value is the brightness of the current point.
facts.d: Analog TV transmits the image line by line; the signal value at a given moment equals the brightness of the point at the same time. TV bandwidth 6.5 / 5.5 MHz gives about 800 points per line.

facts.gist: 1877 Ochorowicz: principles. 1897 Braun: the lamp. 1923 Zworykin: the kinescope. 1928: first regular programme (USA).
facts.d: 1877 Julian Ochorowicz (philosopher, psychologist) defined the general principles of TV; 1897 Ferdinand Braun presented Braun's lamp enabling the kinescope; 1923 Vladimir Zworykin constructed the kinescope; 1928 TV signal sent over the Atlantic and the first US station began regular programmes.

facts.gist: 1934 first experimental broadcast from the Prudential hotel; 1952 first half-hour programme from Warsaw.
facts.d: 1934: first experimental broadcast in Poland, 'Prudential' hotel, Warsaw. 25 October 1952: first half-hour programme from the Institute of Telecommunications in Warsaw, received on 24(!) receivers.
1952: first attempts to record a TV signal (USA). 1953: CCIR (Comité Consultatif International pour la Radio) founded, the forerunner of ITU.

facts.gist: NTSC 1953 (USA), SECAM 1957 (France), PAL 1961 (Germany, Walter Bruch), Telstar 1962, first digital systems 1987.
facts.d: 1953 NTSC (USA), first colour TV standard; 1957 SECAM (France); 1961 PAL by Walter Bruch (Germany); 1962 USA-Europe broadcast via Telstar, the first commercial satellite; 1986 stereo sound; 1987 first digital TV systems (USA / Japan).
Power AC 110/127/220 V, screen 180x240 mm, 625 lines, bands I 49.75-56.25, II 59.25-65.75, III 77.25-83.75 MHz, price 4000 PLN.
Power AC 220 V, screen 220x290 mm, high voltage 12000 V, 625 lines, eight TV channels and four VHF radio sub-ranges, one oval loudspeaker, price 7000 PLN, weight 23 kg.

facts.gist: Brightness, colour, synchronization (start of a line and an image) and sound.
facts.d: The TV signal comprises brightness (luminance), colour (chrominance), synchronizing signals (mark the beginning of a new line and a new image) and sound.

facts.gist: NTSC: 525 lines, 30 FPS. PAL and SECAM: 625 lines, 25 FPS.
facts.d: NTSC (National Television System Committee) 30 FPS, 525 lines; PAL (Phase Alternating Line) 25 FPS, 625 lines; SECAM (Séquentiel couleur à mémoire) 25 FPS, 625 lines.
NTSC: North America, Japan, parts of South America; SECAM: France, Russia / former USSR, parts of Africa; PAL (or PAL/SECAM): most of Europe, Asia, Australia and most other countries.

facts.gist: Analysis (2-D image to 1-D signal) → transmission → reconstruction on the screen.
facts.d: Image analysis: 2D image to 1D signal in the time domain. Signal transmission: transmitter to receiver, usually via radio waves. Image reconstruction: signal back to a 2D image displayed on the screen.

facts.gist: A frame is split into two half-images, odd and even lines, which reduces flicker.
facts.d: The image is scanned with horizontal lines and divided into two half-images (odd lines and even/parity lines); slide 3 links interlacing to reducing flicker. 625 (effective 576) lines, 25 FPS: Europe (PAL/SECAM); 525 (effective 496) lines, 30 FPS: USA (NTSC).

Y voltage is proportional to image brightness. In the monochrome video signal, sync pulses (vertical and per-line horizontal) drop to about -0.25 V, below 0, while picture content reaches about 0.75 V.

facts.gist: Colour is sent as R−Y and B−Y; the receiver adds Y to get the colours back.
facts.d: Colour is carried as colour-difference signals R-Y and B-Y; the receiver recovers colours as Y + (R-Y) = R and Y + (B-Y) = B.
On the slide, a positive signal has black level at U_max and white level at U_min; a negative signal has white level at U_max and black level at U_min.
The spectrum of the TV luminance (vision) signal is concentrated in bands around harmonics of the horizontal scan rate f_h (f_h, 2f_h, ..., n·f_h).

facts.gist: Grids take the video signal, deflection coils take the scan signals and steer the beam; problems: edge geometry and gamma.
facts.d: Colour CRT: three electron beams pass through a shadow mask onto an RGB phosphor grid. Components: cathode, grids (video signal u(t)), deflection coils (scan signals u_h(t), u_v(t)), anode, electron beam, fluorescent screen. Problems: image geometry near the edges and gamma correction.

facts.gist: Compensates the nonlinear voltage-to-brightness curve of the CRT; also suits the eye, which is more sensitive to dark tones.
facts.d: Introduced to compensate the CRT input (voltage) / output (brightness) characteristic; a nonlinear operation encoding/decoding luminance, V_out = A·V_in^γ, usually A = 1 with values 0-1. Human sight is more sensitive to relative differences between darker tones; CRT TVs usually had a maximum luminance of 100 cd/m².

Non-gamma-encoded images allocate too many bits or too much bandwidth to highlights humans cannot differentiate; gamma encoding stores tones more efficiently (example: linear coding with only 32 levels / 5 bits shows coarse dark steps). A camera responds linearly; the eye perceives a tone well below 50% luminance as 50% bright.
Europe: 625 lines per frame, 50 half-images per second; horizontal scan rate f_h = 15625 Hz, vertical scan rate f_v = 50 Hz.

The B&W composite video signal contains luminance, blanking, synchronization and audio signals. One frame = visible lines of the odd half-image, vertical sync / blanking with equalizing pulses, then visible lines of the even half-image.

facts.gist: Picture is AM, sound is FM at a fixed offset. VHF 30–300 MHz, UHF 300–3000 MHz.
facts.d: VHF 30-300 MHz (10 m-1 m), UHF 300-3000 MHz (1 m-10 cm), country dependent. Picture uses amplitude modulation on one frequency; sound uses frequency modulation at a fixed offset, typically 4.5 to 6 MHz.

Tuner (channel selector) to IF amplifier to demodulator/filter giving composite video; sound carrier to FM demodulator, audio amplifier and speaker; video amplifier (brightness, contrast) to CRT; sync separator feeds vertical timebase (V sync) and horizontal timebase (H sync) to flyback transformer (EHT).

facts.gist: Channels lie 8 MHz apart; the video takes 6 MHz and the audio carrier sits 6.5 MHz above the video carrier.
facts.d: Channel separation 8 MHz, video signal bandwidth 6 MHz; video carrier f_w at 0 MHz and audio carrier f_f at +6.5 MHz.

facts.gist: Colour had to work on black-and-white sets and in limited bandwidth, so RGB is sent as Y plus chrominance.
facts.d: Problems: compatibility (colour signal visible on B&W sets) and limited bandwidth; solution: a specific colour coding. RGB is converted to Y (grayscale image) plus chrominance U, V (or I, Q), transmitted, and converted back to RGB.

facts.gist: People do not see fine detail in colour, so chrominance gets less bandwidth than luminance.
facts.d: Humans do not see image details as coloured objects, so chrominance bandwidth can be limited: RGB 6+6+6 = 18 MHz; NTSC Y 4.5 + I 2.0 + Q 1.0 = 7.5 MHz; PAL Y 6 + U 1.2 + V 1.2 = 8.4 MHz.

formulas.name: Luminance (CIE-XYZ based)
formulas.expr: Y = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B  (slides 41-42 print 0.229, a typo; Lecture 1 slides 51-52 use 0.299)

formulas.name: NTSC chrominance (text form)
formulas.expr: I = 0.168 R - 0.257 G - 0.321 B ;  Q = 0.212 R - 0.528 G + 0.311 B  (matrix on same slide shows -0.168 for R in I)

formulas.name: Colour recovery from difference signals
formulas.expr: Y + (R - Y) = R ;  Y + (B - Y) = B ;  slide also writes Y - B + B = G

formulas.name: Gamma correction
formulas.expr: V_out = A * V_in^gamma  (common case A = 1, values in 0-1)

formulas.name: Amplitude modulation
formulas.expr: f(t) = [A + s(t)] sin(2 pi f t + phi)

formulas.name: Frequency modulation
formulas.expr: f(t) = A sin(2 pi [f + s(t)] t + phi)

formulas.name: Receiver passband filter
formulas.expr: f0 ≈ f (filter tuned to carrier frequency)

formulas.name: TV transmitter (video, AM)
formulas.expr: carrier U0 sin(2 pi f_w t) ; output (U0 + u_w(t)) sin(2 pi f_w t)

formulas.name: TV transmitter (audio, FM)
formulas.expr: carrier U0 sin(2 pi f_f t) ; output U0 sin(2 pi (f_w + u_f(t)) t)  (as printed on slide)

formulas.name: Horizontal scan rate (Europe)
formulas.expr: f_h = 625 lines x 25 frames/s = 15625 Hz ; f_v = 50 Hz (50 half-images/s)

formulas.name: Audio carrier position
formulas.expr: f_audio = f_video + 6.5 MHz ; adjacent channel video carriers differ by 8 MHz

traps: PAL and SECAM both use 625 lines / 25 FPS; only NTSC uses 525 lines / 30 FPS.
Effective lines: 576 for PAL/SECAM, 496 for NTSC on the slide (textbooks say about 480).
Channel separation is 8 MHz but video bandwidth is 6 MHz; slide 3 also quotes a TV bandwidth of 6.5 / 5.5 MHz.
The channel table puts the audio carrier at +6.5 MHz, while slide 33 gives a typical range of 4.5-6 MHz.
Picture is AM and sound is FM, not the other way round.
Braun presented the lamp (1897); Zworykin constructed the kinescope (1923); Ochorowicz defined the principles (1877).
SECAM (1957) came before PAL (1961); NTSC (1953) was the first colour standard; CCIR (1953) is an organisation, not a standard.
NTSC needs less total bandwidth (7.5 MHz) than PAL (8.4 MHz) because its luminance band is only 4.5 MHz.
PAL uses U and V; NTSC uses I and Q.
Gamma correction fixes the brightness curve of the CRT, not the geometry near the edges; the eye is more sensitive to differences between dark tones.
Horizontal rate 15625 Hz versus vertical rate 50 Hz; 50 half-images per second versus 25 frames per second.

4.summary: Sampling and bit rates of digital video (ITU-R 601), why compression is needed, terrestrial standards and single frequency networks, UHD and HDR, and the DVB transmission chain: scrambling, Reed-Solomon, interleaving, convolutional coding and QPSK.

facts.gist: Sample at least twice per cycle of the highest frequency and nothing is lost.
facts.d: A sinusoid can be regenerated with no loss of information if it is sampled at least twice per cycle (f_s >= 2 f_max).

facts.gist: SDTV is sampled at 13.5 MHz, HDTV at 74.25 MHz because it has more pixels.
facts.d: SDTV (about 6 MHz video bandwidth) is sampled at 13.5 MHz; HDTV, with many more pixels, at 74.25 MHz.
8 bits per pixel give 2^8 = 256 brightness levels; n bits give 2^n levels.
Y is sampled at 13.5 MHz, CR and CB at 6.75 MHz each; the multiplexed stream runs at 13.5 + 6.75 + 6.75 = 27 MHz.
Luminance: 8 bit x 576 lines x 720 px x 25 fps = 82.944 Mbps. Chrominance (2 x 360 px per line) adds the same, so the total is 165.888 Mbps.

facts.gist: Compression lets digital TV carry 4 to 10 times more programmes than analog in the same channel.
facts.d: Thanks to MPEG-2/MPEG-4 compression, digital TV carries 4 to 10 times more programmes than analog TV in a channel of similar width (up to 10 per channel vs 1).

facts.gist: The digital sampling standard: luminance 13.5 MHz, chrominance 6.75 MHz, for both 625 and 525 lines.
facts.d: Luminance sampled at 13.5 MHz and chrominance at 6.75 MHz. The Shannon minima for 6 MHz and 2.75 MHz bandwidths are 12 MHz and 5.5 MHz; the real rates sit above them for 625/525 compatibility.

facts.gist: SDTV must shrink about 50:1 to fit an 8 MHz channel.
facts.d: To reuse the existing EU UHF transmitters (about 8 MHz), SDTV needs a compression ratio of about 50:1, and HDTV significantly more.

facts.gist: Lossless restores everything; lossy drops some information for good. Digital TV is lossy (MPEG).
facts.d: Lossless compression restores all data; lossy compression permanently removes some. DTV uses lossy compression. MPEG is the umbrella term for the bit-rate reduction standards.
EPG (programme guide), automatic programme search, multi-language sound, subtitles, encoding of paid programmes, interaction, channel lock.

facts.gist: An effective compression.
facts.d: An effective compression: uncompressed SDTV (about 166 Mbps) cannot fit an 8 MHz channel without it.

facts.gist: Analog: NTSC, PAL, SECAM. Digital: DVB (Europe), ATSC (North America), ISDB (Japan, South America).
facts.d: Analog: NTSC, PAL, SECAM. Digital: DVB (Europe), ATSC (North America), ISDB (Japan, South America).
ATSC in North America, ISDB-T in Japan and most of South America, DTMB in China, DVB-T/T2 in Europe, Africa, Russia and Australia.

facts.gist: All transmitters use one frequency; supported by DVB-T and ISDB-T, not by ATSC.
facts.d: SFN is supported by DVB-T and ISDB-T but not by ATSC. DVB-T allows SDTV, not HDTV, mobile reception.

facts.gist: Full HD 1920×1080, 4K UHD 3840×2160, 8K UHD 7680×4320; each step has four times the pixels.
facts.d: Full HD 1920x1080 (2.07 MPx), 4K UHD 3840x2160 (8.29 MPx), 8K UHD 7680x4320 (33.18 MPx): 8K has 16x the pixels of Full HD.

facts.gist: 8K at 120 Hz progressive with 22.2 surround sound.
facts.d: 7680x4320, 16:9, 120 Hz progressive, 12 bits per colour RGB with HDR, 22.2 surround (24 channels), about 50 Mbps with HEVC, 144 Gbit/s uncompressed.
From smallest to largest: Rec. 709 (HDTV) < DCI-P3 (cinema) < Rec. 2020 (UHD).

facts.gist: HDR10: static metadata. HDR10+ and Dolby Vision: dynamic. HLG: no metadata.
facts.d: HDR10: 10-bit PQ, static metadata. HDR10+ and Dolby Vision: dynamic (scene/frame) metadata. HLG: Hybrid Log-Gamma, no metadata. SL-HDR1: SDR base plus reconstruction data.

facts.gist: DVB-S satellite, -C cable, -T terrestrial, -CA conditional access (pay TV), -SI service information, -RC return channels.
facts.d: DVB-S satellite, DVB-C cable, DVB-T terrestrial, DVB-CA common interface for conditional access, DVB-SI service information, DVB-RC return channels.

facts.gist: Scrambling → outer coding → interleaving → inner coding → baseband shaping → QPSK.
facts.d: Scrambling -> outer coding (Reed-Solomon) -> interleaving -> inner coding (convolutional) -> baseband shaping -> QPSK modulation (ETS 300 421).

facts.gist: Mixes data with a pseudo-random sequence to spread the energy; it is not encryption.
facts.d: Packets are randomized (modulo-2 with a pseudo-random sequence, 1503 bytes) to disperse energy and avoid an apparently unmodulated carrier. It is not encryption.

facts.gist: RS(204, 188, 8): adds 16 bytes per packet and corrects up to 8 errors.
facts.d: RS(204, 188, 8): a 188-byte packet becomes 204 bytes (16 parity bytes) and up to 8 byte errors can be corrected.

facts.gist: Spreads burst errors apart so that they become single, correctable errors.
facts.d: A convolutional interleaver spreads burst errors missed by the inner decoder so that after deinterleaving they become isolated, correctable errors.

facts.gist: A convolutional code; puncturing leaves bits out to raise the code rate.
facts.d: Basic code rate 1/2 with constraint length K = 7; puncturing raises it to 2/3, 3/4, 5/6 or 7/8.
Neighbouring Gray code words differ in only one bit; pulse edges are then filtered (shaped) before modulation.

facts.gist: Quadrature Phase Shift Keying: four carrier phases, two bits each.
facts.d: Each carrier phase (pi/4, 3pi/4, 5pi/4, 7pi/4) carries a pair of bits: 4 states = 2 bits per symbol.

formulas.name: Nyquist (Shannon) sampling
formulas.expr: f_s >= 2 * f_max   (6 MHz -> > 12 MHz, 2.75 MHz -> > 5.5 MHz)

formulas.name: Reed-Solomon redundancy
formulas.expr: 204 - 188 = 16 parity bytes; corrects t = 8 byte errors

formulas.name: RS worked example
formulas.expr: error value = S1 - check1 (28 - 26 = 2); position = (S2 - check2) / value ((67 - 63) / 2 = 2)

traps: 13.5 MHz is the SDTV (ITU-R 601) luminance rate; 74.25 MHz is HDTV; 6.75 MHz is each chroma channel; 27 MHz is the multiplexed total.
12 / 5.5 MHz are only the Shannon minima; the real ITU-R 601 rates are 13.5 / 6.75 MHz.
Scrambling disperses energy (not encryption); conditional access (DVB-CA) handles pay-TV encryption.
Interleaving spreads burst errors; scrambling spreads energy. Do not swap them.
RS(204,188,8): 16 bytes are added but only 8 errors are corrected.
The outer code (Reed-Solomon) comes before the inner code (convolutional); modulation is always last.
ATSC has no SFN support; DVB-T and ISDB-T do.
HDR10 = static metadata; HDR10+ and Dolby Vision = dynamic; HLG = none.
4K UHD is 3840x2160 (8.29 MPx); 4096x2160 is cinema 4K and is not on the slide.

5.summary: The baseline JPEG pipeline step by step (colour conversion, 8x8 blocks, DCT, quantization, zig-zag scan, DPCM and run-length plus Huffman coding) and the newer formats: JPEG XR, WebP, BPG, HEIF, FLIF and JPEG XL.

facts.d: JPEG = Joint Photographic Expert Group, formed 1986 by ISO (International Standard Organisation) and CCITT (Comité Consultatif International de Téléphonie et Télégraphie); ISO standard in 1991 (per slide).

facts.gist: Lossy approximates the original; lossless restores it exactly.
facts.d: Lossy compression removes 'excess' data and decompresses by approximating the original (approximate reconstruction). Lossless decompression restores the original data; nothing is permanently modified or lost (exact reconstruction).

facts.gist: Images change slowly, low frequencies matter most, and the eye hardly notices lost high frequencies.
facts.d: JPEG exploits limitations of human eyesight for high compression ratios, lets the user choose quality/compression level, and has optional interlacing and progressive modes. Insights: content changes slowly; within an 8x8 block intensity does not change significantly; lower spatial frequencies carry more information; the eye does not quickly notice loss of high frequencies.

facts.gist: Colour conversion → blocks → DCT → quantization → zig-zag → entropy coding.
facts.d: 1 conversion to luminance-chrominance model (colour images only), 2 division into blocks, 3 DCT f(x,y) -> F(u,v), 4 quantization of DCT coefficients (constant or table), 5 zig-zag array-to-vector conversion, 6 entropy coding (DPCM for DC, RLC for AC, Huffman tables).

facts.gist: RGB becomes luminance Y and chrominance U, V.
facts.d: RGB is converted to Y, U, V tables according to BT.601: Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B; U = -0.147R - 0.289G + 0.436B; V = 0.615R - 0.515G - 0.100B. Y is luminance, U and V are chrominance.

facts.gist: Each plane is cut into blocks of 8 × 8 pixels.
facts.d: Y, U, V arrays are scaled to integers and divided into macroblocks of 8 x 8, f(x,y) with x, y = 0..7.

facts.gist: The DCT turns pixels into frequencies; rows first, then columns.
facts.d: DCT converts an 8x8 block from the spatial domain to the frequency domain. A 2D transform is done as two series of 1D transforms: rows, then columns. Sorting example (2,3,1,2,2,0,1,1,0,1,0,0) -> occurrences (4,4,3,1): spatial information lost, frequency information gained.

facts.gist: DC is the first coefficient, F(0,0); the other 63 are AC.
facts.d: F(0,0) is the DC component; all remaining F(i,j) are AC components (63 per block).

Uniform 'plane' block: only the DC coefficient is significant. 'Chessboard' block: large coefficients also in the high-frequency (lower-right) corner, and after JPEG coding/decoding it is badly distorted, whereas the photorealistic block looks almost unchanged.

facts.gist: Fewer bits per coefficient. This is the main loss in JPEG.
facts.d: Quantization reduces the number of bits per sample; 101101 = 45 -> 4 bits 101100 = 44 -> 3 bits 101000 = 40. The more bits truncated, the more precision lost. Quantization error is the main source of lossy compression.

facts.gist: The eye sees low frequencies best. Uniform: one constant. Non-uniform: a table.
facts.d: Eye is most sensitive to low frequencies (upper-left of the frequency matrix) and less to high frequencies (lower-right). Uniform quantization: Q(u,v) constant; non-uniform: quantization tables.

facts.gist: Two default tables, luminance and chrominance; custom ones can go into the file header.
facts.d: The standard defines two default tables, luminance and chrominance; custom tables can be included in the image header. Luminance table starts 16, 11, 10, 16, ... and ends 99 (max 121); chrominance table starts 17, 18, 24, 47 and is mostly 99 (slide labels chrominance as 'I and Q').

F(0,0) = 1204.7 with Q = 16 gives F^Q(0,0) = 75; F(0,1) = 137.2 / 11 gives 12. Decoding: f* = Integer round(DCT^-1(F^Q * Q)); f*(0,0) = 183 vs original 186, so the reconstruction is close but not exact.

facts.gist: Reads the 8 × 8 matrix into a vector, low frequencies first, so the zeros gather at the end (Tescher, 1978).
facts.d: Zig-zag algorithm (A. G. Tescher 1978) maps the 8x8 matrix to a 1x64 vector [DC, AC1, ..., AC63], low frequencies first, high at the end. Example vector: [75, 12, 18, -1, 15, -2, -2, 2, 10, 1, -2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, -2, -3, -3, 1, 0, ..., 0].

facts.gist: Replaces fixed-length symbols by variable-length codes: frequent = short.
facts.d: DC is coded for the array of blocks; AC1..AC63 for each block. Entropy coder replaces each fixed-length input symbol by a variable-length prefix codeword whose length is proportional to the negative logarithm of its probability.

facts.gist: Differential Pulse Code Modulation: codes the difference from the previous block, which is usually small.
facts.d: Differential Pulse Code Modulation codes the difference between the DC of the current and previous 8x8 block (DC is large but close to the previous one; smaller number -> fewer bits). Δ0 = DC^0, Δi = DC^i - DC^(i-1). Example 45, 54, 48 -> 45, 9, -6; 32, 36 -> 4. Δ vector is Huffman-coded with Table 1.

DC Size codes: 0 -> 00, 1 -> 010, 2 -> 011, 3 -> 100, 4 -> 101, ..., 11 -> 1 1111 1110 (range -2047..2047). Code = Huffman code for Size + additional bits. Example: DC 75, previous 71, Δ = 4, Size = 3, code 100 011 (as on slide).

facts.gist: AC coefficients become pairs (number of zeros, next value); (0,0) ends the block.
facts.d: RLE example: scan line of 67 characters becomes 12W1B12W3B24W1B14W (18 characters). AC vectors have many zeros, especially at the end; RLE codes them as (skip, value): skip = number of zeros, value = next non-zero component; (0,0) = end of block. Example 0,0,0,0,0,1 -> (5,1).

facts.gist: Each AC value is coded as (run length, size) plus its amplitude, with a Huffman code.
facts.d: Each AC_i is coded as Symbol-1 = (Runlength, Size) and Symbol-2 = (Amplitude). Runlength = zeros between AC_i and previous non-zero AC; Size = range of AC_i; Amplitude = value of AC_i. Huffman code is used, like for DC.
Fragment ..., 0, 0, -2: Size of -2 is 2, (Runlength, Size) = (2,2) -> 11111001 from Table 2, amplitude -2 with Size 2 -> 01 from Table 3; result 11111001 01.

Coder: source 8x8 blocks -> DCT -> Quantization (quantisation tables) -> Bit encoder (Huffman code tables) -> compressed data. Decoder: compressed data -> Bit decoder -> Dequantization -> DCT^-1 -> 8x8 data blocks.
Test image 256 x 256 x 8 = 524 288 bits = 64 kB; BMP 66,616 B. JPEG: high compression 24,295 B, middle 31,526 B, low 56,956 B.

facts.gist: Microsoft (first Windows Media Photo, 2006); lapped transform, lossy and lossless.
facts.d: Introduced 2006 as Windows Media Photo, JPEG XR standard 2009; Microsoft technology standardized as ISO/IEC 29199 and ITU-T T.832. Integer-based lapped transform, lossy and lossless, progressive decoding; 8/16/32-bit incl. HDR; TIFF-based file structure; HD Photo precursor.

facts.gist: Google, 2010; lossy mode uses VP8 intra prediction, in a RIFF container.
facts.d: Google, introduced 30 September 2010 as developer preview; RIFF container, .webp. Lossy = VP8 intra-frame prediction; lossless = transforms + LZ77 + entropy coding. 8-bit, lossy colour YUV 4:2:0; alpha and animation; lossless and transparency arrived after the initial lossy release.

facts.gist: Better Portable Graphics, Fabrice Bellard, 2014; based on HEVC.
facts.d: Better Portable Graphics, December 2014, Fabrice Bellard; .bpg format based on a subset of HEVC (H.265). 8-14 bits per channel; grayscale, RGB, YCgCo, CMYK, YCbCr 4:2:0/4:2:2/4:4:4. Web use needs a software/JavaScript decoder; HEVC patent licensing can affect deployment.

facts.gist: HEIF: MPEG container used by Apple, often with HEVC. FLIF: lossless format with MANIAC coding.
facts.d: HEIF (High Efficiency Image File Format): spec June 2015, Apple adoption 2017 (iOS 11, macOS High Sierra); MPEG container ISO/IEC 23008-12 on ISOBMFF; codec decides compression (HEIC commonly HEVC); separates storage from coding. FLIF (Free Lossless Image Format): Sept 2015, FLIF16 Sept 2016; Jon Sneyers and Pieter Wuille; MANIAC adaptive arithmetic coding with context trees; 1-16 bits per channel; ideas continued via FUIF into JPEG XL.

facts.gist: 2021; can recompress existing JPEG files and restore them byte for byte.
facts.d: JPEG XL: 2021, ISO/IEC 18181, reference library libjxl; lossy VarDCT and modular (lossless) coding; HDR, alpha, animation, layers, progressive; existing JPEG files can be recompressed losslessly and restored byte-for-byte. Comparison table: ISOBMFF base container for HEIF and JPEG XL, TIFF for JPEG/Exif and JPEG-XR/TIFF, RIFF for WebP; PNG and GIF have no lossy compression.

formulas.name: Image as array
formulas.expr: f = f(x,y), x = 0..N-1, y = 0..M-1; grey: f(x,y) in {0..S}; colour: f(x,y) = [r(x,y), g(x,y), b(x,y)]

formulas.name: DCT normalisation
formulas.expr: C(u) = 1/sqrt(2) for u = 0, 1 for u != 0 (same for C(v))

formulas.name: Sample transform (cumulative sum)
formulas.expr: F^T(w) = sum_{n=w..8} f(n); all-ones 8x8 block gives 64 in upper-left, 1 in lower-right

formulas.name: DPCM
formulas.expr: Δ0 = DC^0; Δi = DC^i - DC^(i-1), i = 1..m

traps: LOWER spatial frequencies carry more information; high frequencies are less useful detail and noise (easy to reverse in a NOT question).
The DCT itself is not lossy; quantization error is the main source of loss.
Encoding divides by Q(u,v); multiplying by Q(u,v) is the decoding (dequantization) step.
DPCM codes DC coefficients and RLE codes AC coefficients, not the other way round.
EOB = zeros to the end of the block (code 1010, pair (0,0)); ZRL = run of 16 zeros (15 zeros and AC = 0, code 11111111001).
Uniform quantization = one constant Q; non-uniform = quantization tables.
Two default quantization tables (luminance and chrominance), not three RGB tables; luminance starts at 16, chrominance at 17.

Sibling formats: WebP = Google, VP8, RIFF; JPEG XR = Microsoft, TIFF, lapped transform; BPG = Bellard, HEVC; HEIF = MPEG container on ISOBMFF; FLIF = MANIAC; JPEG XL = ISO/IEC 18181, lossless JPEG recompression.

6.summary: Where JPEG loses data, chroma subsampling and the quality factor, the four JPEG modes, entropy, Huffman and arithmetic coding, LZW and DEFLATE, and when to use GIF, TIFF, PNG, WebP or AVIF.

facts.d: Raw size = width x height x bytes per pixel: 1000 x 800 x 3 B = 2.4 MB for 24-bit RGB.

facts.gist: 64 pixels give 64 coefficients: 1 DC (the block average) and 63 AC.
facts.d: One 8x8 block of 64 pixels gives 64 coefficients: 1 DC (F(0,0), the block average) and 63 AC.

facts.gist: Only in chroma subsampling and quantization. The DCT and entropy coding lose nothing.
facts.d: Only chroma subsampling and quantization are lossy, quantization being the main one. The DCT is invertible and entropy coding is lossless.

facts.gist: 4:4:4 full colour; 4:2:2 half horizontally; 4:2:0 half both ways (image 50 % smaller, usual in JPEG).
facts.d: For a 4x2 area: 4:4:4 = 24 samples, 4:2:2 = 16 (-33 %), 4:2:0 = 12 (-50 % of the whole image, -75 % of chroma data). 4:2:0 is the usual JPEG choice.
Lower quality -> larger Q values -> more zero coefficients -> smaller file, with visible blocking.

facts.gist: Almost every JPEG is sequential, Huffman-coded and 8-bit.
facts.d: Almost all real JPEG files are sequential + Huffman + 8-bit; arithmetic coding and 12-bit samples exist but are rarely supported.

facts.gist: Sequential (baseline), progressive, lossless, hierarchical.
facts.d: Sequential (baseline), progressive, lossless and hierarchical. Wavelets belong to JPEG 2000, not to these modes.

facts.gist: One pass, left to right and top to bottom; every decoder must support it.
facts.d: Single pass, left to right, top to bottom. Baseline must be implemented by every JPEG decoder.

facts.gist: Several scans. Spectral selection: low frequencies first. Successive approximation: the top bits first.
facts.d: Several scans add detail: spectral selection sends low-frequency bands first; successive approximation sends all coefficients a few bits at a time from the MSB. Both can be combined.

facts.gist: Predicts each pixel from its neighbours and stores only the error; no DCT, about 2:1.
facts.d: Predictive coding: no DCT and no quantization; only the prediction error X - P is entropy-coded. Typical ratio about 2:1 for colour images.
With A = left, B = above, C = upper-left: P1 = A, P2 = B, P3 = C, P4 = A + B - C, P5 = A + (B - C)/2, P6 = B + (A - C)/2, P7 = (A + B)/2.

facts.gist: A pyramid of resolutions: the small image first, then refinements.
facts.d: A 'super-progressive' pyramid of resolutions: the lowest is coded first and each up-sampled result predicts the next level.

facts.gist: Entropy is the lowest possible average code length; Huffman stays within one bit of it.
facts.d: For a Huffman code the average length L satisfies H <= L < H + 1, where H is the source entropy.

facts.gist: Merge the two rarest symbols again and again; frequent symbols get short, prefix-free codes.
facts.d: Repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes under a new node; frequent symbols get short codes. The code is prefix-free, so it decodes unambiguously.
Cr = Vnc / Vc. In the 44-symbol example a fixed 3-bit code (132 b) became 118 b, so Cr = 1.12.
Huffman needs 23 bits vs 33 bits for a fixed 3-bit code (ratio 1.43); the entropy bound is about 22.4 bits.

facts.gist: Huffman: whole bits, one code per symbol. Arithmetic: one number for the whole message, fractions of a bit.
facts.d: Huffman spends a whole number of bits (at least 1) per symbol; arithmetic coding maps the whole message to one number in [0, 1) and can use fractional bits.
Arithmetic coding is attributed to Peter Elias (1960s). Huffman coding dates from 1952.
Register overflow, growing precision for long strings, binary conversion, and the code word is known only after encoding ends.

facts.gist: LZW (GIF, TIFF): dictionary built on the fly. DEFLATE (PNG, ZIP): LZ77 + Huffman.
facts.d: LZW (GIF, TIFF) builds its dictionary on the fly without sending it. DEFLATE = LZ77 back-references + Huffman (PNG, ZIP, gzip); PNG applies row filters (Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) first.

facts.gist: 256 colours, LZW, simple animation; from UNISYS and CompuServe.
facts.d: Graphics Interchange Format by UNISYS and CompuServe for modem transfer; LZW, 8-bit only (256 colours); GIF89a adds simple animation.

facts.gist: Tagged Image File Format from Aldus; lossless unless the JPEG tag is used.
facts.d: Tagged Image File Format by Aldus Corp. (1980s), later Microsoft; stores many image types and is lossless unless the JPEG tag is used.

facts.gist: Replaces GIF: transparency, gamma, better compression, full colour, but no animation.
facts.d: Designed to replace GIF: alpha channel, gamma correction, 2-D interlacing, 5-25 % better compression. No animation (only via APNG).

facts.gist: WebP: Google, VP8-based, 25–35 % smaller than JPEG. AVIF: AV1-based, HDR, slower to encode.
facts.d: WebP (Google, 2010): VP8-based lossy plus lossless, alpha, animation, about 25-35 % smaller than JPEG. AVIF: AV1 intra coding, HDR and wide gamut, slower to encode.
GIF, WebP and AVIF support animation; PNG (APNG extension only), JPEG and TIFF do not.

facts.gist: JPEG-LS: prediction. JPEG 2000: wavelets. JPEG XL: recompresses JPEGs. JPEG AI: learned coding.
facts.d: JPEG XL recompresses existing JPEGs losslessly (about 20 % smaller); JPEG-LS is prediction-based (LOCO-I); JPEG 2000 uses wavelets; JPEG AI uses learned coding.

facts.gist: Photos: JPEG, WebP, AVIF. Graphics and screenshots: PNG. Simple animation: GIF, WebP.
facts.d: Photos -> JPEG/WebP/AVIF; graphics and screenshots -> PNG; simple animations -> GIF/WebP.

formulas.name: Raw image size
formulas.expr: size = W * H * bytes_per_pixel   (1000 * 800 * 3 B = 2.4 MB)

formulas.name: Lossless JPEG residual
formulas.expr: Diff = X - P   (P4 = A + B - C)

formulas.name: Average code length
formulas.expr: L = sum p_i * l_i   (A8 B4 C2 D2 -> 28/16 = 1.75 bit)

formulas.name: Arithmetic interval update
formulas.expr: low' = low + range * cumLow(s);  range' = range * p(s)

traps: The DCT is invertible; the loss comes from rounding after division by Q (quantization).
Spectral selection = frequency bands first; successive approximation = bits from the MSB first.
Progressive = several scans at one resolution; hierarchical = a pyramid of resolutions.
Huffman merges the two LOWEST frequencies, never the highest.
Huffman needs at least 1 bit per symbol; arithmetic coding can spend fractions of a bit.
LZW belongs to GIF and TIFF; DEFLATE (LZ77 + Huffman) belongs to PNG and ZIP.
GIF: 256 colours and animation; PNG: 24-bit plus alpha but no animation.
TIFF came from Aldus; GIF came from UNISYS and CompuServe.
Lossless JPEG reaches about 2:1, lossy JPEG about 10-20:1.

7.summary: Spatial and temporal redundancy, I, P and B frames and GOPs, motion estimation and compensation, rate control, quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, VMAF), codec generations, containers and adaptive streaming.

facts.gist: VCEG and MPEG write HEVC (JCT-VC) and VVC (JVET); the royalty-free line is VP8, VP9, AV1, AV2.
facts.d: ITU-T VCEG and ISO/IEC MPEG build main-line codecs in joint teams: JCT-VC (HEVC) and JVET, the Joint Video Experts Team (VVC). The open line is VP8, VP9, AV1, AV2.

facts.gist: Rate = width × height × bits per pixel × frames per second. Raw UHD is about 12 Gbit/s, so video must be compressed.
facts.d: UHD 3840x2160, 24 bit per pixel, 60 fps needs about 11.9 Gbit/s, roughly 12 times a 1 Gbit/s Ethernet link.

facts.gist: Spatial: DCT, intra prediction. Temporal: motion compensation, the biggest gain. Perceptual: subsampling, quantization. Statistical: entropy coding.
facts.d: Spatial (DCT, intra prediction), temporal (motion-compensated prediction), perceptual (chroma subsampling, quantization), statistical (VLC/Huffman, CABAC). Temporal is new in video and gives the largest gain.

facts.gist: Chroma subsampling and quantization lose data; entropy coding does not.
facts.d: Chroma subsampling and quantization are lossy; entropy coding (VLC, Huffman, CABAC) is lossless.

facts.gist: Colour at half resolution both ways: 1.5 samples per pixel, half the data.
facts.d: 4:2:0 keeps 1.5 samples per pixel: the whole image shrinks by 50 % (chroma data by 75 %); 4:2:2 shrinks it by 33 %.

facts.gist: PSNR in dB, SSIM 0–1 (structure), VMAF 0–100 (Netflix, learned), MOS 1–5 (viewers).
facts.d: PSNR = 10 log10(MAX^2/MSE), about 30-45 dB for lossy video; SSIM 0-1 (structure, contrast, luminance); VMAF 0-100 (Netflix 2016, learned fusion); MOS 1-5 (viewer tests).

facts.gist: Bit-rate difference at equal quality; −40 % means 40 % fewer bits.
facts.d: Bit-rate difference at equal quality: (R_test - R_ref) / R_ref. 6 vs 10 Mbit/s gives -40 %, i.e. 40 % saving.

facts.gist: Quantized residual, motion vectors and modes, headers. Never the reference frames themselves.
facts.d: Quantized residual DCT coefficients, motion vectors and modes, and headers. The decoder rebuilds the reference frames itself.

facts.gist: Sequence → GOP → picture → slice → macroblock (16×16, motion) → block (8×8, DCT).
facts.d: Sequence -> GOP (random access) -> Picture -> Slice (resync) -> Macroblock (16x16 luma, unit of motion) -> Block (8x8, unit of the DCT). A 4:2:0 macroblock has 6 blocks (4 Y + Cb + Cr).

facts.gist: I: own pixels only, random access. P: from the previous anchor. B: from both sides, compresses most, never a reference in MPEG-2.
facts.d: I = intra only, about 10:1; P = predicted from the previous anchor, about 20:1; B = from previous and next anchors, about 50:1. In MPEG-2 B-frames are never references.

facts.gist: Number of frames divided by the sum of 1/ratio for every frame. It is not the plain average of the ratios.
facts.d: Average = N / sum(1/ratio_i). IBBPBBPBBPBB with 10:20:50 gives about 29:1, not the 39:1 of a plain average.

facts.gist: Only the bitstream and the decoder; how the encoder searches is free.
facts.d: Only the bitstream and the decoder. The motion-search method, matching criterion (usually SAD) and search window are left to the encoder.

facts.gist: The encoder does the costly motion search; the decoder only copies blocks.
facts.d: Only the encoder pays for motion search; the decoder just copies the block the vector points to. Cheap decoders, expensive encoders.

facts.gist: 25 tests instead of 225 for ±7 pixels, at the risk of missing the best match.
facts.d: For a +/-7 window TSS needs 9 + 8 + 8 = 25 SAD evaluations vs 15 x 15 = 225 for full search, at the risk of a local minimum.
MPEG-2 1/2 pel, AVC 1/4, HEVC 1/4, AV1 1/8, VVC 1/16 pel.

facts.gist: The encoder predicts from the decoded frame, because that is all the decoder has; otherwise they drift apart.
facts.d: The encoder predicts from decoded (not original) frames; otherwise encoder and decoder drift apart until the next I-frame.

facts.gist: They see background that appears later, average out noise and can be quantized harder.
facts.d: They see uncovered background in the future frame, averaging two predictions cancels noise, and as non-references they can be quantized harder.

facts.gist: B-frames need the next anchor first, so it is sent earlier. DTS = when to decode, PTS = when to show.
facts.d: Display I1 B2 B3 P4 ... is sent as I1 P4 B2 B3 P7 B5 B6: each anchor goes before the B-frames that need it. DTS says when to decode, PTS when to show.

facts.gist: Closed: no prediction across the border, clean cuts. Open: slightly more efficient. Long GOP: better compression, slower seeking.
facts.d: A closed GOP has no prediction across its border (clean cuts, ad splicing, ABR segments); an open GOP lets leading B-frames use the previous GOP. An IDR empties the reference buffer.

facts.gist: CBR: broadcast. Two-pass VBR: disc and VOD. CRF: constant quality, size unknown. Capped CRF: streaming.
facts.d: CBR -> broadcast multiplex (DVB); 2-pass VBR -> disc and VOD; CRF/CQ -> archives (size unknown); capped CRF -> streaming ladders.
AVC 9 directions, HEVC 35 modes, VVC 67 modes (plus MIP, CCLM). MPEG-2 predicts only the DC coefficient.

facts.gist: MPEG-2 → AVC → HEVC → VVC: each needs roughly half the bits, with a more complex encoder.
facts.d: AVC vs MPEG-2: about 50 % less at about 4x complexity. HEVC vs AVC: 40-50 % less, encoder up to 10x. VVC vs HEVC: 30-50 % less at several times the complexity.
Relative to MPEG-2 = 100: AVC 50, HEVC 28, AV1 20, VVC 16. Each generation saves about 30-50 %.

facts.gist: The codec compresses; the container (MP4, MKV, TS) packs and time-stamps tracks. The extension names no codec.
facts.d: A container (MP4/ISO BMFF, MKV, TS) multiplexes and time-stamps tracks; the codec compresses. The .mp4 extension says nothing about the codec; check with ffprobe.

facts.gist: HLS and DASH: 2–6 s segments, each starting with an IDR; the player picks the quality.
facts.d: HLS and MPEG-DASH cut video into 2-6 s segments, each starting with an IDR, with aligned closed GOPs across renditions.

facts.gist: PQ: absolute brightness, HDR10. HLG: backward compatible, broadcast.
facts.d: PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) up to 10 000 cd/m2; HLG is backward compatible and meant for broadcast. HDR10 metadata is static (per film), HDR10+ and Dolby Vision dynamic (per scene).
-crf 23 = constant quality (file size unknown); -g 12 = GOP length 12; -bf 2 = two B-frames between anchors.
MPEG-4 Part 10 = AVC, Part 14 = MP4; MPEG-H Part 2 = HEVC, Part 12 = HEIF; MP3 = MPEG-1 Audio Layer III.

formulas.name: Raw data rate
formulas.expr: R = W * H * bits_per_pixel * fps   (3840*2160*24*60 = 11.9 Gbit/s)

formulas.name: PSNR
formulas.expr: PSNR = 10 * log10( MAX^2 / MSE )   [dB], MAX = 255 for 8 bit

formulas.name: BD-rate
formulas.expr: BD = (R_test - R_ref) / R_ref   at equal quality

traps: B-frames compress the MOST (about 50:1), I-frames the least (about 10:1).
Average GOP compression is a harmonic mean, N / sum(1/C), not the plain average of the ratios.
Macroblock (16x16) is the unit of motion; block (8x8) is the unit of the DCT.
MPEG standardizes the bitstream and the decoder, never the encoder's motion search.
Transmission (decode) order differs from display order because B-frames need the next anchor first.
Closed GOP = no prediction across the border; open GOP = leading B-frames use the previous GOP.
SSIM is 0-1, VMAF 0-100, MOS 1-5, PSNR in dB (about 30-45).
HLG is backward compatible for broadcast; PQ is the absolute curve used by HDR10.
A container is not a codec: .mp4 may hold H.264, HEVC or AV1.
-crf sets constant quality, not a bit rate; -g sets the GOP length.

questions.q: The 'optical triad', i.e. what is needed to see color, consists of:
o: transmission, reflection and absorption of the light
hue, saturation and value of the observed surface
light, an object (matter) and the human visual system
cones, rods and the optic nerve leading to the brain
questions.hint: Picture the slide drawing: a bulb, a box and an eye.
questions.r: Slide 5 lists light, object (matter) and the human visual system as the Optical Triad. Transmission, reflection and absorption are the ways matter interacts with light (slide 10), not the triad.
questions.why: bold label 'Optical Triad'; opening slide of the perception part

questions.q: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength of approximately:
questions.hint: Ultraviolet sits just below it and infrared just above it; the narrower version on the slide is 400–700 nm.
questions.r: Slide 6: λ = 380–780 nm (roughly 400–700 nm). Below about 380 nm is ultraviolet, above about 780 nm is infrared.
questions.why: explicit numeric range with arrow on the slide

questions.q: The refractive index, which characterizes the transmission of light through a material, is defined as:
o: the speed of light in the material divided by its speed in a vacuum
the fraction of incident light absorbed per unit thickness
the speed of light in a vacuum divided by its speed in the material
the ratio of reflected light energy to incident light energy
questions.hint: Water has an index of 1.333, so for a slower medium the ratio must be greater than 1.
questions.r: Slide 11: RI = speed of light in a vacuum / speed of light in the material (water RI = 1.333). The inverted ratio would give values below 1 (about 0.75 for water).
questions.why: bold 'refractive index' plus a numeric example

questions.q: According to the lecture, the human retina contains approximately:
o: 100–120 million cones and 6–9 million rods
6–9 million cones and 6–9 million rods
1–2 million cones and 500 million rods
6–9 million cones and 100–120 million rods
questions.hint: The receptors for night vision far outnumber the receptors for color.
questions.r: Slides 16 and 18: cones 6–9 million (avg. 4.5 million as printed), rods 100–120 million (avg. 90 million as printed). Swapping the two numbers is the classic trap. The printed averages fall below the ranges; that is how the slide states them.
questions.why: numbers repeated on two slides (text and table)

questions.q: In photopic (daytime) vision, which receptors are involved in recognizing light stimuli?
o: Only the cones
Only the rods
Rods and cones in equal proportion
Mainly rods, assisted by ganglion cells
questions.hint: Daytime vision is color vision.
questions.r: Slide 19 (highlighted in red): in photopic vision only the cones, which enable color vision, are involved. Rods dominate scotopic (night) vision, where the world is seen in shades of gray.
questions.why: red highlighted text 'only the cones ... are involved'

questions.q: The Purkinje phenomenon means that as light levels decrease:
o: blues appear darker than other colors
reds appear darker than other colors
all colors keep their relative brightness
greens appear darker than other colors
questions.hint: Think of the geranium photos fading at dusk; the eye's peak sensitivity moves toward shorter wavelengths.
questions.r: Slides 20-21: the Purkinje phenomenon is a disturbance in the perception of color brightness in low light, so reds appear darker than other colors. Peak sensitivity shifts from 555 nm (photopic) to 507 nm (scotopic), away from red, not away from blue.
questions.why: two dedicated slides with a photo example

questions.q: Hemeralopia is:
o: a condition that impairs vision in relatively dim light
the darkening of reds as light levels decrease
the inability to see in bright light
the loss of color perception caused by cone damage
questions.hint: The slide defines it as the opposite of night blindness.
questions.r: Slide 22: hemeralopia is the opposite of nyctalopia, i.e. the inability to see in bright light. Impaired vision in dim light is nyctalopia (night blindness).
questions.why: paired terms give ready sibling distractors

questions.q: In the Munsell color system, VALUE, CHROMA and HUE correspond respectively to:
o: saturation, lightness and hue
lightness, hue and saturation
hue, lightness and saturation
lightness, saturation and hue
questions.hint: CHROMA is about how far a color is from gray.
questions.r: Slide 25: VALUE = lightness, CHROMA = saturation, HUE = measured hue. Chroma is the difference between a pure color and gray, so it is saturation, not lightness.
questions.why: three bold terms with arrows

questions.q: Which set contains only the five PRIMARY hues of the Munsell system?
o: R, Y, G, B, P
YR, GY, BG, PB, RP
R, G, B, C, M
C, M, Y, K, R
questions.hint: Munsell has 5 + 5 hues; the intermediate ones are named by joining two neighbours.
questions.r: Slide 26: the 5 primary hues are red, yellow, green, blue and magenta/purple (R, Y, G, B, P). YR, GY, BG, PB, RP are the 5 intermediate hues. Cyan is not a Munsell primary.
questions.why: list of 5 + 5 hues fits the classify format

questions.q: The abbreviation CIE (as in the CIE-XYZ model) stands for:
o: Comité International de l'Électronique
Commission Internationale de l'Échelle
Color Imaging and Encoding
Commission Internationale de l'Éclairage
questions.hint: In English it is the International Commission on Illumination.
questions.r: Slide 30: CIE = Commission Internationale de l'Éclairage (International Commission on Illumination), which ran the 1931 color-matching experiment.
questions.why: expansion given in English and French; matches the common 'X stands for' question style

questions.q: Why was the CIE-RGB model considered inconvenient, which led to new fictitious XYZ primaries?
o: Its primaries lie outside the visible spectrum
Its matching functions take negative values
It cannot express the luminance of a color
It requires four primaries instead of three
questions.hint: Look at the red curve on the 1931 experimental graph dipping below zero.
questions.r: Slides 33-34: matching all spectral colors needed negative weights (or additional colors), so CIE-RGB was inconvenient; fictitious XYZ primaries let all visible colors have non-negative components. The RGB primaries (700, 546.1, 435.8 nm) are real visible wavelengths.
questions.why: bold italic 'inconvenient -> there are negative weights'

questions.q: Which statement about the CIE XYZ coordinates is TRUE?
o: X represents luminance, while Y and Z encode hue
XYZ are real primary lights of 700, 546.1 and 435.8 nm
Y represents luminance; X and Z are never negative
Z represents luminance, while X and Y may be negative
questions.hint: The same letter carries brightness in xyY and in YUV.
questions.r: Slide 34: Y represents luminance (linked to cone sensitivity), and X and Z are chosen so that all visible colors are represented without negative components. 700/546.1/435.8 nm were the real RGB primaries of the 1931 experiment; the XYZ primaries are fictitious.
questions.why: bold 'luminance' and italic 'non-negative' on the slide

questions.q: In the CIELAB model, a negative value of the b coordinate indicates:
o: blue
yellow
green
red
questions.hint: b is the blue–yellow axis and a is the green–red axis; in each name the negative end comes first.
questions.r: Slide 41: b is the blue–yellow axis (negative = blue, positive = yellow); a is the green–red axis (negative = green, positive = red). L runs from 0 (black) to 100 (reference white).
questions.why: explicit axis sign list on the slide

questions.q: In the HSV model, hue (H) is expressed as:
o: an angle from 0° to 360°
a distance from the gray axis
a height along the cone axis
a value between black and white
questions.hint: Think of a colour wheel.
questions.r: Slide 44: H is an angle around the cone (0–360°). Saturation is the distance from the gray axis and Value the position along it; S and V run from 0 to 1.
questions.why: ranges in the first bullet

questions.q: The HSL color space is represented as:
o: a single cone whose axis is the gray axis
a cube whose diagonal runs from black to white
a sphere with lightness from 0 to 100
a double cone with pure hues at lightness 1/2
questions.hint: Black at one tip, white at the other, saturated colors around the 'equator'.
questions.r: Slide 46: HSL is a solid composed of two cones; fully saturated colors lie on a circle with lightness 1/2 (0 = black, 1 = white), resembling the perceptual Munsell system. A single cone is HSV, the cube is RGB/CMY and the 0–100 sphere is CIELAB.
questions.why: sibling-model shapes make natural distractors

questions.q: Which statement about the RGB model is TRUE?
o: It is additive; its cube diagonal runs from black to white
It is subtractive; its cube diagonal runs from white to black
It models how inks mix when printing on white paper
Its main advantage is describing an imagined color easily
questions.hint: Think of a monitor: no light at all gives black.
questions.r: Slide 47: RGB is additive, the diagonal [0,0,0]–[1,1,1] is the grayscale axis from black to white, and it models displaying images on a monitor. Its advantage is ease of reproducing a described color; describing an imagined color is its disadvantage. Printing on white paper is the CMY (subtractive) model.
questions.why: title 'additive model' plus advantage/disadvantage lines

questions.q: Which statement about the YCbCr model is TRUE?
o: It is the 'analog' model used in PAL broadcasting
Its chrominance ranges from -1 to 1 around zero
It is a scaled and shifted YUV used in JPEG/MPEG
It is derived from YIQ to match NTSC receivers
questions.hint: Note the '+ 0.5' in its Cb and Cr formulas.
questions.r: Slide 53: YCbCr is a scaled and shifted YUV used with JPEG/MPEG compression; YUV is 'analog' and YCbCr is 'digital', and YCbCr chrominance always takes values in [0, 1]. PAL uses YUV, NTSC uses YIQ.
questions.why: list of properties; YUV vs YCbCr confusion stated on the slide

questions.q: According to the 'psychological paradox' of color temperature:
o: low color temperature is perceived as cold (blue)
high color temperature is perceived as warm (orange)
color temperature has no effect on perceived warmth
low color temperature is perceived as warm (orange)
questions.hint: A candle flame is about 1,800 K; a clear blue sky in deep shadow is about 8,000–10,000 K.
questions.r: Slide 57: a low color temperature gives light perceived as warm (yellow, orange) and a high color temperature gives light perceived as cold (cool blue), the reverse of physical heat, hence 'paradox'.
questions.why: marked '(!)' on the slide

questions.q: Which set contains only properties of ROD cells?
o: high acuity, low sensitivity, fast reaction, three types
low acuity, very high sensitivity, slow reaction, one type
low acuity, low sensitivity, fast reaction, three types
high acuity, very high sensitivity, slow reaction, one type
questions.hint: Rods trade detail and speed for sensitivity in the dark.
questions.r: Slide 18 table: rods have low acuity, very high sensitivity (diffuse light), slow reaction to light and one type across the spectrum (scotopic vision). Cones have high acuity, low sensitivity, fast reaction and three types (photopic vision).
questions.why: comparison table; easy to turn into classify or NOT questions

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of the CIE-XYZ chromaticity diagram?
o: It contains information about the brightness of a color
Pure spectral colors lie on the envelope of the graph
Other visible colors lie inside the graph
White is at point C (x = 0.333, y = 0.333)
questions.hint: The diagram is a 2-D projection; which of the three XYZ quantities was dropped?
questions.r: Slide 37 states in red that the diagram does not contain information about brightness (it excludes luminance); a color is given only by [x, y]. The other three options are listed properties.
questions.why: red 'does not contain' text on the slide

questions.q: In the CMY model, the point [0, 0, 0] corresponds to:
o: white
black
medium gray
pure cyan
questions.hint: RGB adds light and CMY subtracts it. What does [0, 0, 0] mean in each model?
questions.r: Slide 49: the CMY cube diagonal [0,0,0]–[1,1,1] is the gray scale from white to black, the reverse of RGB, where [0,0,0] is black. CMY models color subtraction, e.g. printing on white paper.
questions.why: RGB and CMY diagonals are mirror images; classic reversal trap

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as an advantage of YCoCg over YCbCr?
o: Simpler and faster calculations
Better correlation of color planes, so better compression
Lossless reversibility of the transform
Closer match to colors as perceived by the human eye
questions.hint: The listed advantages are about computation and compression, not perception.
questions.r: Slide 55 lists three advantages: simpler and faster calculations, better correlation of color planes (better color compression) and lossless reversibility. Matching human perception is the reason given for YIQ's I and Q (slide 52), not for YCoCg. YCoCg = luminance Y, chrominance orange Co, chrominance green Cg.
questions.why: explicit three-item advantage list

questions.q: Which pairing of television color model and TV system is correct?
o: YUV – NTSC, YIQ – PAL
YUV – SECAM, YIQ – PAL
YCbCr – PAL, YIQ – SECAM
YUV – PAL, YIQ – NTSC
questions.hint: The model with I and Q belongs to the American standard.
questions.r: Slide 51: YUV – PAL TV system; slide 52: YIQ – NTSC TV system, downward compatible with black-and-white TV where only Y is used. Swapping the two is the obvious trap.
questions.why: slide headings; easy swap distractor

questions.q: Which advantage does the lecture attribute to the HSV model?
o: Ease of reproducing a described color
Easy, interactive description of an imagined color
Precise, device-independent color representation
Lossless conversion to RGB using fewer bits
questions.hint: RGB and CMY share the opposite weakness.
questions.r: Slide 44: HSV's advantage is the ability to easily and interactively generate a description of an imagined color, which is exactly the disadvantage of RGB and CMY (whose advantage is reproducing a described color). Device independence belongs to CIELAB; lossless fewer-bit conversion belongs to YCoCg.
questions.why: advantage/disadvantage lines for RGB, CMY and HSV mirror each other

questions.q: As ambient light decreases, vision enters a transitional phase with a partial or gradual loss of color perception. This is called:
o: photopic vision
scotopic vision
mesopic vision
hemeralopia
questions.hint: Greek 'meso' means middle.
questions.r: Slide 19: mesopic vision is the transitional phase between photopic vision (only cones, full color) and scotopic vision (minimal light, shades of gray). Hemeralopia is the inability to see in bright light.
questions.why: three-term definition slide; reversed ask of a definition

questions.q: The D65 standard used in computer graphics corresponds to a color temperature of about:
questions.hint: It is described as a slightly cloudy sky, a bit cooler than the noon sun.
questions.r: Slide 58: 6,500 K is a slightly cloudy sky (D65 standard in computer graphics), perceived as cool daylight with a blue tint. 2,700–3,000 K is a tungsten bulb, 5,000–5,500 K is noon sun, 8,000–10,000 K is clear blue sky in deep shadow.
questions.why: table of values with D65 named explicitly

questions.q: In the YUV model, the Y component carries:
o: the brightness, i.e. a grayscale image
the difference between the blue and red parts
the saturation of each colour
the amount of yellow in the image
questions.hint: Black-and-white sets used only this one.
