questions.r: Slide 51: Y is luminance, the brightness that forms the grayscale image. U and V carry the colour (chrominance). Y does not stand for yellow.

questions.q: Why do television colour models separate luminance from chrominance?
o: The eye is more sensitive to brightness than to colour
The eye is more sensitive to colour than to brightness
Screens can show brightness and colour only in turn
Cameras record brightness and colour on two sensors
questions.hint: Which errors do you notice first?
questions.r: Slide 51: people notice errors in luminance more than in chrominance, so the colour part can be compressed more.

questions.q: In CIELAB, the value ΔE expresses:
o: how different two colours look
how bright a colour is on paper
how pure a single colour is
how warm a light source is
questions.hint: It is a distance between two points.
questions.r: Slide 43: ΔE is the distance between two colours in L, a, b. A smaller ΔE means a closer colour match.

questions.q: What is the main strength of CIELAB compared with RGB or HSV?
o: It is device-independent and close to human perception
It is the easiest way to describe an imagined colour
It directly drives the subpixels of a computer display
It needs only two numbers for any visible colour
questions.hint: Print has to match the screen.
questions.r: Slide 41: CIELAB is a device-independent transformation of CIE XYZ and is approximately perceptually uniform. Easy description is the advantage of HSV; RGB drives displays.

questions.q: CMY is called subtractive because its colours arise when inks:
o: absorb parts of white light
emit red, green and blue light
reflect all parts of light equally
change the wavelength of light
questions.hint: Think of printing on white paper.
questions.r: Slide 49: CMY models colour subtraction, as in printing: each ink removes (absorbs) part of the white light. Emitting light is the additive RGB case.

questions.q: A rough, matte surface shows mainly:
o: diffuse reflection
specular reflection
complete transmission
complete absorption
questions.hint: A mirror is the opposite case.
questions.r: Slide 12: a rough surface scatters light in many directions (diffuse). A perfect mirror is specular; a mix of both is most common in practice.

questions.q: On the CIE chart, the line from white point C through colour A to the edge gives:
o: the dominant wavelength of A
the complementary colour of A
the brightness of colour A
the color temperature of A
questions.hint: It continues on the side of A.
questions.r: Slide 38: from C through A to the envelope gives the dominant wavelength. Going from A through C to the opposite edge gives the complementary colour. The chart has no brightness.

questions.q: The color temperature of a light source is defined by comparison with:
o: a heated black body
the noon sun on a clear day
a perfectly white reflector
a standard candle flame
questions.hint: The object does not really exist.
questions.r: Slide 57: it is the temperature (in K) to which a perfect black body must be heated to give light of the same colour. Such a body does not exist.

questions.q: In scotopic (night) vision, the world is seen:
o: in shades of gray
in full but dim colour
mostly in blue and green
mostly in red and orange
questions.hint: Which receptors work at night?
questions.r: Slide 19: under minimal light only the rods work, so the world is perceived in shades of gray.

questions.q: The three types of cones differ in:
o: the wavelengths they respond to
the brightness they can stand
the direction of light they accept
the shapes they recognise
questions.hint: They are called S, M and L.
questions.r: Slide 16: S, M and L cones have their peak sensitivity at short (blue), medium (green) and long (red) wavelengths.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the digital camera pipeline shown in the lecture?
o: Lens → ADC → Sensor/CFA → DSP → Storage
Lens → Sensor/CFA → DSP → ADC → Storage
Lens → Sensor/CFA → ADC → DSP → Storage
Sensor/CFA → Lens → ADC → Storage → DSP
questions.hint: Light must be focused before it reaches the silicon, and a processor can only work on numbers, not on voltages.
questions.r: Light passes the lens, is captured by the sensor with its colour filter array, is digitized by the ADC, processed by the DSP and then stored. Putting the DSP before the ADC is wrong because the DSP works on digital data.
questions.why: dedicated pipeline diagram that summarizes the whole acquisition section

questions.q: In the camera controls table, aperture is the control that changes:
o: the exposure duration and the motion blur
the signal gain and the rendered brightness
the angle of view for a given sensor size
the amount of light and the depth of field
questions.hint: Think of the iris of the eye: an opening that gets wider or narrower.
questions.r: Aperture controls the light reaching the sensor and the depth of field. Exposure duration and motion blur belong to shutter speed, gain to ISO, and angle of view to focal length.
questions.why: table of four controls; the sibling rows are ready-made distractors

questions.q: Changing the aperture setting from f/16 to f/2.8 results in:
o: a narrower aperture and a larger depth of field
a wider aperture and a shallower depth of field
a wider aperture and a larger depth of field
a narrower aperture and a shallower depth of field
questions.hint: The f-number is a fraction of the focal length: f/2.8 is a bigger fraction than f/16.
questions.r: A smaller f-number means a wider aperture (slide 8), and f/2.8 gives a shallow depth of field while f/16 gives a large one (slide 9). The usual trap is assuming a smaller number means a smaller opening.
questions.why: two slides (8 and 9) with explicit f/2.8 vs f/16 labels

questions.q: Which statement about ISO is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: It changes signal gain and does not increase the light collected
It widens the aperture so that more light reaches the sensor
It lengthens the exposure so that more light reaches the sensor
It reduces the visible noise when it is set to a higher value
questions.hint: ISO acts after the light has already arrived, like turning up the volume on a quiet recording.
questions.r: Slide 11 states that ISO changes signal gain and does not increase the light collected. Higher ISO increases visible noise (ISO 3200 vs ISO 200 on slide 12), so the last option is reversed.
questions.why: explicit sentence on slide 11 plus noise comparison on slide 12

questions.q: CCD stands for:
o: Colour-capture diode
Charge-coupled device
Charge-conversion detector
Complementary-coupled device
questions.hint: The name describes how charge packets are passed from one cell to the next, like a bucket brigade.
questions.r: CCD = charge-coupled device: light generates charge in photosensitive pixels and the charge is transferred to an output amplifier. 'Complementary' belongs to the CMOS acronym, not CCD.
questions.why: acronym expanded on the slide; 'X stands for' questions are common

questions.q: The first CCD, designed in 1969 for data storage, was created by:
o: W. Boyle and G. Smith at Bell Labs
Fairchild Electronics engineers
Canon's sensor research team
Fujifilm's Super CCD team
questions.hint: The same telephone-company research lab that also gave us the transistor.
questions.r: Boyle and Smith (Bell Labs) designed the first CCD in 1969, originally for data storage. Fairchild Electronics came later (1974) with the first CCD used for image acquisition.
questions.why: bold dated milestone list; matches the 'was created by' question style

questions.q: In the lecture's CCD vs CMOS (APS) comparison, which pairing is correct?
o: CCD: pixel-level conversion; CMOS: charge transfer
CCD: often digital output; CMOS: analog voltage
CCD: integrated circuitry; CMOS: external circuitry
CCD: charge transfer; CMOS: pixel-level conversion
questions.hint: Recall the CCD's name: charge is coupled and moved across the chip, while CMOS does the work at each pixel.
questions.r: The table gives CCD readout = charge transfer (analog voltage output, more external circuitry) and CMOS readout = pixel-level conversion (often digital output, often integrated circuitry). The other options swap the two columns.
questions.why: comparison table; swapped columns are an easy distractor set

questions.q: The Bayer colour filter array uses, in each 2 × 2 block:
o: two red, one green and one blue filter
two blue, one red and one green filter
two green, one red and one blue filter
one red, one green, one blue and one emerald filter
questions.hint: The colour our eyes are most sensitive to gets double representation; the mosaic is written G-R-G-B.
questions.r: The Bayer pattern uses two green, one red and one blue filter (G-R-G-B, the most popular mosaic scheme). Red-green-blue-emerald describes the RGBE filter.
questions.why: bold CFA sentence plus 'most popular mosaic scheme (G-R-G-B)'

questions.q: Which set contains only colour filter arrays that include magenta filters?
o: Bayer and RGBE
RGBE and CMYY
Bayer and CYGM
CMYY and CYGM
questions.hint: Look for the letter M in the filter names.
questions.r: CMYY (cyan, magenta, yellow, yellow) and CYGM (cyan, yellow, green, magenta) both contain magenta. Bayer (G-R-G-B) and RGBE (red, green, blue, emerald) contain none.
questions.why: four named CFA patterns on one slide; fits the 'which set contains only' style

questions.q: The Fujifilm Super CCD (1999) differs from a conventional sensor because it:
o: uses octagonal photosites, raising horizontal and vertical resolution
stacks blue, green and red photodiodes at different silicon depths
bonds the pixel layer onto a separate high-speed logic layer
uses rectangular pixels covered by a CMYY colour filter array
questions.hint: Its pixels have eight sides and the grid is turned by 45 degrees.
questions.r: Super CCD uses octagonal rather than rectangular pixels, giving higher horizontal and vertical resolution at the expense of diagonal resolution. Stacking colour photodiodes by depth describes the Foveon X3; bonding to a logic layer describes stacked CMOS.
questions.why: text bullets with an explicit trade-off (diagonal resolution)

questions.q: The Foveon X3 sensor obtains colour information by:
o: placing a G-R-G-B mosaic of filters over the pixels
stacking three layers at different depths in silicon
using octagonal photosites arranged in a diagonal grid
reading each pixel through its own amplifier and converter
questions.hint: Blue light is absorbed near the surface of silicon, red light goes deepest.
questions.r: The Foveon X3 is a layered sensor: blue, green and red sensors are stacked (blue on top, red at the bottom) because silicon absorbs different wavelengths at different depths. A G-R-G-B mosaic is the Bayer CFA.
questions.why: dedicated Bayer vs Foveon slide with absorption-depth diagram

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a task of the in-camera digital signal processor (DSP)?
o: Analog-to-digital quantization of the sensor signal
Colour interpolation (demosaicing)
Image enhancement and colour correction
Image compression and computational photography
questions.hint: The DSP works only on data that is already digital. Which step must happen before it?
questions.r: Slide 23 lists demosaicing, enhancement and colour correction, compression and computational photography. A/D conversion is done earlier by the separate ADC block (slides 4 and 22).
questions.why: bulleted list of DSP functions; NOT-form predicted variant

questions.q: A 64 GB SD card belongs to which capacity standard?
o: SD
SDHC
SDXC
SDUC
questions.hint: SDHC stops at 32 GB; the next class goes all the way up to 2 TB.
questions.r: SDXC covers more than 32 GB up to 2 TB. SDHC covers more than 2 GB up to 32 GB, and SDUC more than 2 TB up to 128 TB.
questions.why: list of capacity thresholds; applied as a predicted variant

questions.q: Which statement about stacked CMOS sensors is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: Stacking guarantees a global shutter, removing all distortion
Pixel and logic chips are bonded vertically; distortion can remain
Stacking always increases dynamic range regardless of design
Stacking makes fabrication and bonding simpler and cheaper
questions.hint: The slide explicitly warns against reading too much into the word 'stacked'.
questions.r: Pixel and logic chips are bonded vertically (some designs add memory). Faster readout reduces rolling-shutter distortion, but stacked does not imply global shutter, so distortion can remain; dynamic range depends on the design and fabrication is more complex.
questions.why: advantages vs trade-offs slide with explicit warnings

questions.q: According to the lecture, image quality is jointly determined by:
o: aperture, shutter speed and ISO
megapixels, sensor format and card speed
sensor type, ADC bit depth and file format
lens, sensor and image processing engine
questions.hint: Follow the light from the front of the camera to the chip that produces the final image.
questions.r: Slide 28 shows Lens → Sensor → Image processing engine, and the key takeaways say optics, sensor and processing jointly shape image quality. Aperture, shutter speed and ISO are exposure controls.
questions.why: dedicated slide plus repeated on the key takeaways slide

questions.q: An image histogram shows:
o: the brightness of the pixels along one row
how many pixels have each intensity level
how many pixels are darker than the average
the strength of each spatial frequency
questions.hint: 'card' means cardinality: you are counting the members of a set.
questions.r: Slide 29: a histogram counts the pixels at each intensity level. It says nothing about where the pixels are; spatial frequencies belong to the Fourier spectrum.
questions.why: formula box; roadmap goal 'interpret image histograms'

questions.q: An image histogram in which many pixels reach level 255 indicates:
o: shadow clipping, i.e. an underexposed image
low contrast concentrated in the midtones
highlight clipping, i.e. an overexposed image
strong periodic noise in the frequency domain
questions.hint: 255 is the brightest value an 8-bit pixel can hold.
questions.r: Many pixels at 255 means highlight clipping, i.e. overexposure. The opposite case on the same slide (many pixels near levels 6-7) indicates underexposure.
questions.why: two worked histogram examples with arrows to the conclusion

questions.q: Histogram equalization redistributes pixel intensities using:
o: the DFT magnitude spectrum
a normalized Gaussian mask
the median of a 3 × 3 window
the cumulative histogram
questions.hint: The mapping keeps the order of intensities and adds up counts as you move from dark to bright.
questions.r: The slide states that histogram equalization redistributes intensities using the cumulative histogram. Gaussian masks and medians are spatial filters from the image processing section.
questions.why: defining sentence at the top of the slide

questions.q: Which statement about the FFT is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: It is a separate transform using only cosine basis functions
It captures both the location and scale of local image detail
It is a fast algorithm for computing the DFT, not a new transform
It is the transform behind block-based JPEG compression
questions.hint: Read the bold line under the transforms table.
questions.r: The slide states in bold: FFT is a fast algorithm for computing the DFT, not a different transform. Cosine basis and JPEG belong to the DCT; location and scale belong to the wavelet transform.
questions.why: bold sentence on the slide

questions.q: Which pairing of transform and typical use is correct?
o: FFT: JPEG compression; DCT: periodic-noise removal
DCT: JPEG compression; DWT: multiscale analysis
DWT: JPEG block compression; FFT: denoising
DCT: multiscale analysis; DWT: periodic-noise removal
questions.hint: JPEG splits the image into blocks of cosine patterns; wavelets look at detail at several scales.
questions.r: The table gives FFT for frequency filtering and periodic-noise removal, DCT for JPEG compression and energy compaction, and DWT for denoising, multiscale analysis and compression.
questions.why: three-column comparison table of FFT, DCT and DWT

questions.q: A Gaussian filter computes each output pixel as:
o: a weighted average of its neighbourhood, with weights summing to 1
the fifth value of its 3 × 3 neighbourhood, sorted by brightness
the maximum value found in its 3 × 3 neighbourhood, to remove dark noise
the cumulative histogram value of its own intensity
questions.hint: The centre pixel counts most and the neighbours count less, but it is still an average.
questions.r: A Gaussian filter replaces each pixel with a weighted average of its neighbourhood, and the mask is normalized so its weights sum to 1. Taking the fifth sorted value is the median filter.
questions.why: defining sentence plus formula box; roadmap goal 'compare Gaussian and median'

questions.q: The median filter replaces each pixel with:
o: the average of its 3 × 3 neighbourhood
the middle value of its sorted 3 × 3 neighbourhood
the brightest value of its 3 × 3 neighbourhood
a weighted sum of all nine values of its 3 × 3 neighbourhood
questions.hint: Nine values in a row, sorted: pick the one exactly in the middle.
questions.r: Slide 42: the pixel and its 8 neighbours are sorted and the middle (fifth) value is taken. An average or weighted sum is what a Gaussian-type filter does.
questions.why: two-step algorithm in a box

questions.q: To remove isolated dark spots from an otherwise uniform image, the lecture's examples favour:
o: median filtering, which removed the spots completely
Gaussian filtering, which removed them without blurring
histogram equalization, which spread the intensities
a sharpening filter, which boosts the fine detail
questions.hint: One filter averages outliers into their neighbours; the other simply outvotes them.
questions.r: Slide 43 shows the median filter turning a white image with isolated black pixels into a clean white image. Gaussian smoothing averages dark values into their neighbours and blurs fine detail (slide 41) instead of removing them.
questions.why: summary slide discussion question: median or Gaussian filtering, and why?

questions.q: Which statement about high dynamic range (HDR) imaging is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: Bracketed exposures can capture shadow and highlight detail
One stop more exposure halves the light that is collected
HDR represents a narrower range of scene brightness
HDR is obtained from a single exposure at maximum ISO
questions.hint: Think of the -4, -2, +2 and +4 stop photos of the same night scene.
questions.r: HDR represents a wider range of scene brightness, and bracketed exposures capture shadow and highlight detail. One stop more exposure doubles, not halves, the light collected.
questions.why: three short bullet facts; roadmap goal 'explain HDR'

questions.q: A digital image is:
o: a two-dimensional array of pixel values
a list of the frequencies in a scene
a continuous function of light intensity
a set of equations that describe shapes
questions.hint: It has a width N and a height M.
questions.r: Slide 3: a digital image is a 2-D array f(x, y); each value is a gray level, a colour or a colour index.

questions.q: In a camera, the analog-to-digital converter (ADC):
o: quantizes the analog signal into a digital code
fills in the two missing colours of every pixel
moves the charge from pixels to the amplifier
limits the light that reaches the sensor
questions.hint: Look at its name.
questions.r: Slide 22: the ADC quantizes an analog signal into a digital code; more bits give more levels. Filling in colours (demosaicing) is done later by the DSP.

questions.q: Demosaicing is needed because, behind a colour filter array, each pixel:
o: records only one colour
records three colours in turn
records only brightness changes
records the colours of its neighbours
questions.hint: Two of the three values are missing.
questions.r: Slides 16 and 23: every pixel lies under one colour filter, so the DSP interpolates the missing colours (colour interpolation, demosaicing).

questions.q: A colour filter array (CFA) is:
o: a mosaic of colour filters over the sensor pixels
a stack of three sensor layers, one for each colour
a set of lenses that separate colours by angle
a table that maps pixel values to screen colours
questions.hint: Bayer is the best-known example.
questions.r: Slide 16: a CFA places colour filters over the sensor pixels. Stacked layers are the Foveon X3 idea.

questions.q: RAW data from a camera is:
o: sensor data recorded without conversion
an image compressed with the DCT in blocks
an image after white balance
a reduced preview of the photo
questions.hint: Nothing has been done to it yet.
questions.r: Slide 23: RAW is recorded without conversion by the processing engine; JPEG is compressed and TIFF is processed but uncompressed.

questions.q: For the same sensor, a shorter focal length gives:
o: a wider angle of view
a narrower angle of view
a higher signal amplification
a longer exposure time
questions.hint: Compare a 20 mm and a 500 mm lens.
questions.r: Slides 5 and 7: focal length sets the angle of view, and shorter lenses see wider. Gain is ISO and exposure time is the shutter speed.

questions.q: Shutter speed controls:
o: exposure duration and motion blur
angle of view and image magnification
signal gain and visible noise
bit depth and number of levels
questions.hint: Think of flowing water.
questions.r: Slide 5: shutter speed changes exposure duration and motion blur; focal length the angle of view; ISO the signal gain.

questions.q: A side effect of Gaussian filtering is that it:
o: blurs detail
adds bright spots
clips the highlights
shifts the colours
questions.hint: Averaging has a price.
questions.r: Slide 40: each pixel becomes a weighted average of its neighbourhood, which smooths noise but also fine detail.

questions.q: One stop more exposure means that the light collected:
o: doubles
triples
is halved
stays equal
questions.hint: It is the photographic step.
questions.r: Slide 44: one stop more exposure doubles the light collected.

questions.q: What does the wavelet transform (DWT) offer that the Fourier transform does not?
o: both the location and the scale of detail
the magnitude and the phase of frequencies
cosine patterns inside blocks of 8 × 8
a faster way to compute the same DFT
questions.hint: Multiscale analysis is its main use.
questions.r: Slide 33: the DWT captures location and scale. The Fourier spectrum is global, with limited spatial localization; cosine blocks are the DCT.

questions.q: In 1877, the general principles of television were defined by:
o: Ferdinand Braun
Vladimir Zworykin
Julian Ochorowicz
Walter Bruch
questions.hint: The earliest date on the timeline belongs to a Pole who was neither an engineer nor a physicist.
questions.r: Slide 4: in 1877 Julian Ochorowicz, philosopher and psychologist, defined the general principles of television. Braun came 20 years later (1897, Braun's lamp), Zworykin built the kinescope in 1923 and Bruch defined PAL in 1961.
questions.why: first entry of the history timeline, bold year

questions.q: Which statement about the kinescope is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: Braun's lamp (1897) enabled it; Zworykin constructed it in 1923
Zworykin's lamp (1897) enabled it; Braun constructed it in 1923
Ochorowicz constructed it in 1877 after defining TV principles
Braun constructed it in 1928 for the first transatlantic broadcast
questions.hint: The lamp came first (end of the 19th century); the working tube came in the 1920s. Match each name to the right decade.
questions.r: Slide 4: in 1897 physicist Ferdinand Braun presented Braun's lamp, which enabled the construction of a kinescope; in 1923 Vladimir Zworykin constructed the kinescope. The second option swaps the two inventors; 1928 is the year of the transatlantic TV transmission.
questions.why: two dated inventor entries on one slide, classic swap target

questions.q: The first standard of colour television was:
o: SECAM, introduced in France in 1957
NTSC, introduced in the USA in 1953
PAL, introduced in Germany in 1961
CCIR, introduced in Europe in 1953
questions.hint: The 'first' belongs to the same country that started the first regular TV programme in 1928.
questions.r: Slide 6: 1953 - USA, NTSC standard, first standard of colour television. SECAM (1957) and PAL (1961) came later; CCIR (1953) was an association, the forerunner of ITU, not a colour standard.
questions.why: slide explicitly labels it 'first standard of color television'

questions.q: In 1961 the PAL colour transmission standard was defined in Germany by:
o: Vladimir Zworykin
Max Wertheimer
Ferdinand Braun
Walter Bruch
questions.hint: Not a kinescope pioneer and not a psychologist: look for the only name on the timeline tied to the 1960s.
questions.r: Slide 6: 1961 - Germany, Walter Bruch defines the transmission standard PAL (Phase Alternating Line). Zworykin built the kinescope (1923), Braun presented his lamp (1897) and Wertheimer described the phi phenomenon (1912).
questions.why: named inventor + year + acronym on one bullet

questions.q: Which sequence lists the events in the correct chronological order?
o: SECAM standard → NTSC standard → PAL standard → Telstar satellite broadcast
NTSC standard → PAL standard → SECAM standard → Telstar satellite broadcast
NTSC standard → SECAM standard → PAL standard → Telstar satellite broadcast
NTSC standard → SECAM standard → Telstar satellite broadcast → PAL standard
questions.hint: The American standard came first, and the satellite link came one year after the last of the three colour standards.
questions.r: Slide 6: NTSC 1953 (USA), SECAM 1957 (France), PAL 1961 (Germany), Telstar broadcast USA to Europe 1962. The usual mistake is placing PAL before SECAM.
questions.why: dated timeline, easy to turn into an ordering item

questions.q: PAL stands for:
o: Picture Amplitude Level
Phase Alternating Line
Phase Amplitude Locking
Progressive Alternate Lines
questions.hint: Something about the colour signal changes from one scan line to the next.
questions.r: Slides 6 and 9: PAL = Phase Alternating Line (Walter Bruch, 1961; 25 FPS, 625 lines). 'Progressive' is wrong because analog PAL uses interlaced scanning.
questions.why: acronym expanded on two slides

questions.q: SECAM stands for:
o: Système Électronique Couleur Avec Modulation
Sequential Colour Amplitude Modulation
Séquentiel Couleur à Mémoire
Signal Électronique Couleur à Mémoire
questions.hint: It is French (1957). Ask what a receiver must do if colour information arrives one piece after another.
questions.r: Slide 9: SECAM = Séquentiel couleur à mémoire ('sequential colour with memory'), the French standard of 1957 with 25 FPS and 625 lines. The other expansions are invented.
questions.why: acronym expanded with bold letters on slide

questions.q: According to the lecture, the NTSC system (USA) uses:
o: 525 lines (496 effective) at 30 FPS
625 lines (576 effective) at 25 FPS
525 lines (576 effective) at 25 FPS
625 lines (496 effective) at 30 FPS
questions.hint: The American system has fewer lines but more frames per second than Europe.
questions.r: Slides 9 and 12: NTSC - 525 lines (effective 496), 30 FPS; PAL/SECAM - 625 lines (effective 576), 25 FPS. Textbooks usually give about 480 visible NTSC lines, but the slide states 496.
questions.why: numbers repeated on slides 9 and 12

questions.q: Which pair of analog colour TV standards both use 25 FPS and 625 lines?
o: NTSC and PAL
NTSC and SECAM
None - each standard differs
PAL and SECAM
questions.hint: Exclude the oldest of the three standards.
questions.r: Slide 9: PAL - 25 FPS, 625 lines; SECAM - 25 FPS, 625 lines; NTSC - 30 FPS, 525 lines. Slide 12 groups them as 'Europe (PAL / Secam)'; they differ in colour coding, not in scanning.
questions.why: three standards with parameters listed side by side

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of the TV signal listed in the lecture?
o: Brightness (luminance)
Error-correction codes
Synchronizing signals
Colour (chrominance)
questions.hint: Recall the four items: two about the picture, one about timing and one you hear.
questions.r: Slide 9: the TV signal comprises brightness (luminance), colour (chrominance), synchronizing signals (marking the beginning of a new line and a new image) and sound. Analog TV carries no error-correction data.
questions.why: bulleted list of four components

questions.q: In analog television, 'image analysis' is:
o: sending the obtained signal from the transmitter to the receiver, usually via radio waves
converting the received signal back into a two-dimensional image shown on the screen
converting a two-dimensional image into a one-dimensional time signal
compensating the nonlinear voltage-to-brightness characteristic of the CRT display
questions.hint: It is the first of the three stages: what happens on the camera side before anything is sent.
questions.r: Slides 11-12: image analysis converts a 2D image into a 1D signal in the time domain. Signal transmission sends it (usually via radio waves), image reconstruction turns it back into a 2D image, and the last option describes gamma correction.
questions.why: italic key term defined on slides 11 and 12

questions.q: In interlaced scanning, the analysed image is:
o: scanned with horizontal lines and divided into two half-images (odd and even lines)
scanned with vertical columns and divided into three colour fields (R, G and B)
scanned with horizontal lines in a single pass, all lines in order in every frame
scanned in square blocks that are transmitted one after another in every frame
questions.hint: 'Inter-laced': two sets of lines woven together, like interlocked fingers.
questions.r: Slide 12: the image is scanned with horizontal lines and divided into two 'half-images', one of odd lines and one of even (parity) lines. Scanning all lines in order in one pass is progressive scanning.
questions.why: slide title + diagram of odd/even half-images

questions.q: Which statement about the monochrome video signal shown in the lecture is TRUE?
o: Sync pulses lie below the picture levels, at about -0.25 V
Sync pulses reach the highest level, at about 0.75 V
Sync pulses carry the brightness of each picture point
Sync pulses appear only once per frame, never per line
questions.hint: Sync must never be mistaken for picture content. Where on the voltage axis would you put it?
questions.r: Slides 14-15: line (horizontal) and vertical sync pulses drop below 0 V to about -0.25 V, while picture content reaches about 0.75 V. Horizontal sync pulses occur for every line, and brightness is carried by the luminance signal.
questions.why: voltage-level diagram with labelled sync pulses

questions.q: Gamma correction was introduced mainly to:
o: preserve image geometry near the edges of the CRT screen
compensate the nonlinear voltage-to-brightness curve of CRTs
reduce the bandwidth needed by the chrominance signals U and V
separate the audio carrier from the video carrier inside a channel
questions.hint: It is a power-law fix applied to a property of the display tube.
questions.r: Slide 26: gamma correction is based on the limitations of CRT televisions and compensates for their input (voltage) / output (brightness) characteristics. Edge geometry is the other CRT problem on slide 25, but gamma does not fix it.
questions.why: dedicated section of four slides

questions.q: Why do gamma-encoded images store tones more efficiently than linearly encoded ones?
o: Eyes are more sensitive to lighter tones; linear coding wastes bits on shadows
Gamma encoding raises the bit depth from 5 bits to 8 bits per sample
Gamma encoding discards chrominance and keeps only the luminance
Eyes are more sensitive to darker tones; linear coding wastes bits on highlights
questions.hint: In the 32-level (5-bit) example, look at which end of the grey ramp shows coarse visible steps with linear coding.
questions.r: Slides 26-28: human sight is more sensitive to relative differences between darker tones than lighter ones, so non-gamma-encoded images allocate too many bits or too much bandwidth to highlights humans cannot tell apart. The reversed statement (lighter tones) is the trap.
questions.why: same idea repeated on slides 26, 27 and 28

questions.q: In an analog TV channel, picture and sound are transmitted as follows:
o: picture by frequency modulation, sound by amplitude modulation at a 4.5-6 MHz offset
picture by amplitude modulation, sound by frequency modulation at a 4.5-6 MHz offset
picture and sound both by amplitude modulation on one common carrier frequency
picture and sound both by frequency modulation at a fixed 0.5-1 MHz offset
questions.hint: Recall the transmitter block diagram: two different modulator boxes, one for each signal.
questions.r: Slides 33-34: picture information uses amplitude modulation (AM) on one frequency; sound uses frequency modulation (FM) at a fixed offset, typically 4.5 to 6 MHz, from the picture signal. The first option swaps the two.
questions.why: stated on slide 33 and drawn on slide 34

questions.q: According to the lecture, the Ultra High Frequency (UHF) band covers:
o: 300-3000 MHz, wavelengths 1 m to 10 cm
30-300 MHz, wavelengths 10 m to 1 m
3-30 MHz, wavelengths 100 m to 10 m
3000-30000 MHz, wavelengths 10 cm to 1 cm
questions.hint: Each band spans one decade of frequency, and UHF sits one decade above VHF. Wavelength in metres ≈ 300 / frequency in MHz.
questions.r: Slide 33: VHF = 30-300 MHz (10 m to 1 m), UHF = 300-3000 MHz (1 m to 10 cm). The second option is VHF; the others are neighbouring bands.
questions.why: table on slide

questions.q: In the European TV channel structure, the channel separation and the video signal bandwidth are:
o: 6 MHz and 8 MHz
8 MHz and 4.5 MHz
7 MHz and 5 MHz
8 MHz and 6 MHz
questions.hint: The whole channel must be wider than its video part, because the audio carrier also has to fit inside it.
questions.r: Slide 37: channel separation - 8 MHz; video signal bandwidth - 6 MHz; the audio carrier sits 6.5 MHz above the video carrier. The swapped pair (6 and 8) is the main trap. Slide 3 separately quotes a TV bandwidth of 6.5 / 5.5 MHz.
questions.why: two key numbers stated under the diagram

questions.q: In analog colour TV, the luminance signal Y is transmitted so that:
o: monochrome sets still show a correct grayscale picture
colour receivers can skip demodulating the chrominance
the audio carrier can sit 6.5 MHz above the video carrier
all three colour components get an equal 6 MHz bandwidth
questions.hint: Think about the millions of TV sets that existed before colour broadcasting began.
questions.r: Slide 41: Y gives a grayscale image that a monochrome receiver reproduces correctly, so colour TV stayed downward compatible with black-and-white sets; colour travels separately in the chrominance signals. Slides 41-42 print the R weight as 0.229, a typo for 0.299 (Lecture 1, slides 51-52).
questions.why: formula box plus the compatibility argument; the same Y formula appears in Lectures 1 and 5

questions.q: Why does green contribute most to the luminance signal Y?
o: The human eye is most sensitive to wavelengths in the green part of the spectrum
The green phosphor of a CRT needs the highest voltage to glow at full brightness
The green signal needs the largest bandwidth of all components in the channel
The green signal is sent on the audio carrier and must therefore be amplified
questions.hint: Slide 18 shows a bell-shaped curve. Where is its peak?
questions.r: Slide 18: the signal should be formed considering the relative sensitivity of the human eye, which peaks in the green region (around 550 nm). So slide 41 gives G the largest weight (0.587). The other reasons do not appear in the lecture.
questions.why: sensitivity curve explains formula weights

questions.q: The word "television" combines:
o: Greek "far" and Latin "the image seen"
Greek "light" and Latin "the screen used"
Greek "fast" and Latin "a moving picture"
Greek "many" and Latin "people watching"
questions.hint: Telephone starts the same way.
questions.r: Slide 3: Greek tele = far, Latin visio = the image seen.

questions.q: The "phi phenomenon" was described in 1912 by:
o: Max Wertheimer
Ferdinand Braun
Vladimir Zworykin
Julian Ochorowicz
questions.hint: The other three built or planned television itself.
questions.r: Slide 3: phi phenomenon – Max Wertheimer, 1912. Braun presented the lamp, Zworykin built the kinescope and Ochorowicz defined the principles of television.

questions.q: In analog TV, the signal value at a given moment equals:
o: the brightness of the point being scanned
the average brightness of the whole scan line
the number of the line being transmitted
the colour of the previous image point
questions.hint: One value, one point.
questions.r: Slide 3: the image is sent line by line, and the signal value at a moment equals the brightness of the point at that time.

questions.q: Sending the even lines first and then the odd lines serves mainly to reduce:
o: flicker
image noise
colour errors
sound delay
questions.hint: More half-images per second look steadier.
questions.r: Slide 3 lists even and odd lines broadcast one after the other under flicker. Half-images double the refresh rate without sending more lines.

questions.q: Synchronizing signals in a TV signal mark:
o: the beginning of a new line and a new image
the brightest and the darkest image point
the change from the picture signal to the sound
the border between two TV channels
questions.hint: The receiver must know where to start.
questions.r: Slide 9: synchronizing signals mark the beginning of a new line and a new image.

questions.q: NTSC stands for:
o: National Television System Committee
North American Television Signal Code
National Transmission Standard Council
New Television Synchronization Concept
questions.hint: It names a group of people.
questions.r: Slide 9: NTSC = National Television System Committee (30 FPS, 525 lines).

questions.q: SECAM was the analog standard of:
o: France and the former USSR
the United States and Japan
Germany and Australia
Brazil and Argentina
questions.hint: It is a French abbreviation.
questions.r: Slide 10: SECAM in France, Russia / the former USSR and parts of Africa; NTSC in North America and Japan; PAL in most other countries.

questions.q: Analog colour TV carries colour as:
o: colour-difference signals such as R−Y and B−Y
three separate full-bandwidth signals R, G and B
hue and saturation values of every image point
cyan, magenta and yellow on separate carriers
questions.hint: The receiver adds Y back.
questions.r: Slide 16: colour is carried as R−Y and B−Y; the receiver recovers R and B by adding Y.

questions.q: In a CRT, the deflection coils:
o: steer the electron beam over the screen
set the brightness of the beam
emit the electrons that form the beam
glow when electrons hit them
questions.hint: They receive the scan signals.
questions.r: Slide 25: the horizontal and vertical scan signals drive the deflection coils. The grids receive the video signal, the cathode emits electrons and the fluorescent screen glows.

questions.q: Why can chrominance be sent with less bandwidth than luminance?
o: People do not see fine image detail in colour
Colour signals travel faster than brightness
Colour is needed only in every second TV frame
Chrominance contains no information on edges
questions.hint: It is about the eye, not the signal.
questions.r: Slide 43: people do not see image details as coloured objects, so the chrominance bandwidth can be limited.

questions.q: In 1962, television was broadcast from the USA to Europe using:
o: the Telstar satellite
an undersea coaxial cable
a chain of radio towers
the first digital system
questions.hint: It was the first commercial one of its kind.
questions.r: Slide 6: 1962 – broadcast from the USA to Europe via Telstar, the first commercial satellite. Digital systems came in 1987.

questions.q: According to the Nyquist theorem as presented in the lecture, a sinusoidal signal can be regenerated with no loss of information if it is sampled:
o: at a frequency of at least once per cycle
at a frequency of at least four times per cycle
at a frequency equal to half of one cycle
at a frequency of at least twice per cycle
questions.hint: Think of the factor that turns a 6 MHz bandwidth into a 12 MHz minimum sampling rate.
questions.r: Slide 8: a sinusoid can be regenerated with no loss if sampled at a frequency greater than or equal to twice per cycle. Once per cycle would make the sinusoid look constant; four times per cycle is more than the minimum.
questions.why: bold term on slide; basis of all later sampling numbers

questions.q: Uncompressed SDTV video needs a bit rate of roughly:
o: 17 Mbps
50 Mbps
166 Mbps
1,660 Mbps
questions.hint: Far more than one 8 MHz channel can carry.
questions.r: Slide 13: luminance and chrominance need about 83 Mbps each, together about 166 Mbps. That is why digital TV depends on compression.
questions.why: final result of worked example

questions.q: In digital SDTV, each chrominance signal has, per line:
o: as many samples as luminance
half as many samples as luminance
twice as many samples as luminance
no samples, only a reference level
questions.hint: The eye needs less colour detail.
questions.r: Slide 13: 720 luminance samples per line, but 360 for each of the two chrominance signals. Two halves together equal the luminance data.
questions.why: predicted variant: asks for the reason behind the worked numbers

questions.q: Thanks to MPEG-2/MPEG-4 compression, digital television can carry how many more programs than analog TV in a channel of similar width?
o: 4 to 10 times more
2 to 3 times more
20 to 50 times more
about 100 times more
questions.hint: Compare with the analog vs digital table: 1 program per analog channel versus 'up to ...' per digital channel.
questions.r: Slide 14: DTV sends 4 to 10 times more programs; slide 20 confirms up to 10 programs per channel versus 1 for analog. The number 50 appears only as the required compression ratio (50:1).
questions.why: bold DTV definition with a specific range; repeated in table on slide 20

questions.q: According to the ITU-R 601 Recommendation, the sampling rates for luminance and chrominance are:
o: 12 MHz and 5.5 MHz
27 MHz and 13.5 MHz
74.25 MHz and 37.125 MHz
13.5 MHz and 6.75 MHz
questions.hint: Chrominance is sampled at exactly half the luminance rate.
questions.r: Slide 15: ITU-R 601 uses 13.5 MHz for luminance and 6.75 MHz for chrominance. 12 MHz and 5.5 MHz are only the Shannon minimum values; 27 MHz is the multiplexed total.
questions.why: named standard with key numbers; repeated on slides 8, 11, 15

questions.q: To use the existing EU UHF transmitters (about 8 MHz of bandwidth), the required compression ratio for SDTV is about:
questions.hint: Uncompressed SDTV is about 166 Mbps, and the 8 MHz channel must still carry more than one program.
questions.r: Slide 16: about 50:1 for SDTV, and significantly more for HDTV. 4:1 and 10:1 echo the '4 to 10 times more programs' statement, which is a different fact.
questions.why: specific ratio stated as a bullet

questions.q: Which statement about compression in digital television is TRUE?
o: DTV uses lossless compression so that all information is restored
Lossy compression restores all of the original data after decompression
DTV uses lossy compression, which permanently eliminates some information
Lossless compression permanently removes information that is not noticeable
questions.hint: Which type of compression can reach a ratio of 50:1? It accepts a loss the viewer may not notice.
questions.r: Slide 17: lossy compression permanently eliminates some information, and 'for DTV lossy compression is used'. Lossless compression keeps all data, but it cannot reach the ratios DTV needs.
questions.why: explicit definitions plus 'for DTV lossy compression is used'

questions.q: MPEG is best described as:
o: an umbrella term for standards with techniques that reduce video bit rate
a modulation method that changes the carrier phase for pairs of bits
an outer error-correction code that turns 188-byte packets into 204
a European consortium that writes the DVB transmission standards
questions.hint: Slide 17 calls it an 'umbrella term'. What kind of techniques does it group?
questions.r: Slide 17: techniques that reduce the bit rate of digital video are incorporated into standards under the umbrella term MPEG. QPSK is the modulation, RS(204,188) is the outer code, and the DVB Project is the consortium.
questions.why: definition with sibling-term distractors

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as an additional function that digital TV provides to the user?
o: Descriptive program information (EPG)
Displaying subtitles
Switching between PAL and SECAM
Encoding of paid TV programs
questions.hint: PAL and SECAM belong to which column of the analog vs digital table?
questions.r: Slide 18 lists EPG, automatic program search, language versions (multi-channel sound), subtitles, encoding of paid TV programs and others (interaction, channel lock). PAL and SECAM are analog TV standards.
questions.why: bulleted list of functions; NOT-form fits list slides

questions.q: According to the lecture, the fundamental problem of digital television is:
o: a single frequency network
an accurate colour gamut
a stable time code (VITC)
an effective compression
questions.hint: Remember the ratio of about 50:1 that SDTV needs.
questions.r: Slide 19: 'Fundamental problem of DTV - an effective compression'. Uncompressed SDTV (about 166 Mbps) does not fit an 8 MHz channel without it.
questions.why: stated as the conclusion under the DTV diagram

questions.q: Which set contains only digital television standards?
o: DVB, PAL, ATSC
ISDB, SECAM, NTSC
NTSC, PAL, SECAM
DVB, ATSC, ISDB
questions.hint: One family comes from the analog era of colour encoding; the other was designed for compressed bit streams.
questions.r: Slide 20: analog standards are NTSC, PAL, SECAM; digital standards are DVB, ATSC, ISDB. Each mixed set contains at least one analog standard.
questions.why: comparison table; classify pattern used in past exams

questions.q: According to the world map of digital terrestrial TV standards, which pairing of region and standard is correct?
o: South America: ISDB-T
North America: DVB-T
China: ATSC
Australia: DTMB
questions.hint: Recall the map colours: green for North America, pink for most of South America and Japan, orange for China, blue for Europe, Africa and Australia.
questions.r: Slide 21: ATSC in North America, ISDB-T in most of South America (and Japan), DTMB in China, DVB-T/DVB-T2 in Europe, Africa, Russia and Australia.
questions.why: map with legend; region-standard pairing is easy to ask

questions.q: According to the service-aspect comparison table, SFN (Single Frequency Network) is supported by:
o: ATSC only
ATSC and DVB-T, but not ISDB-T
DVB-T and ISDB-T, but not ATSC
ISDB-T only
questions.hint: The American system scores worst in most rows of this table.
questions.r: Slide 22: SFN is NO for ATSC and YES for both DVB-T and ISDB-T.
questions.why: YES/NO row in comparison table

questions.q: The resolution and pixel count of 4K UHD given in the lecture are:
o: 4096 x 2160, about 8.85 MPx
3840 x 2160, about 8.29 MPx
2560 x 1440, about 3.69 MPx
questions.hint: 4K UHD is two Full HD widths by two Full HD heights.
questions.r: Slide 25: 4K UHD = 3840 x 2160 = 8.29 MPx. 7680 x 4320 (33.18 MPx) is 8K UHD; 4096 x 2160 is cinema 4K and is not on the slide.
questions.why: resolution chart with exact numbers

questions.q: Which parameter set matches UHD-2 / Super Hi-Vision as described in the lecture?
o: 7680 x 4320, 50 Hz interlaced, 7.1 surround sound
3840 x 2160, 60 Hz interlaced, 5.1 surround sound
1920 x 1080, 120 Hz progressive, 22.2 surround sound
7680 x 4320, 120 Hz progressive, 22.2 surround sound
questions.hint: Super Hi-Vision is the 8K system. Think of the highest frame rate and the multi-layer audio system.
questions.r: Slide 26: 7680 x 4320, 16:9, 120 Hz progressive, 12 bits per colour RGB with HDR, 22.2 surround sound (24 channels), 50 Mbps with H.265/HEVC, 144 Gbit/s uncompressed.
questions.why: bold parameter list

questions.q: On the CIE 1931 colour space diagram, which order lists the colour gamuts from smallest to largest?
o: Rec. 709 < DCI-P3 < Rec. 2020
DCI-P3 < Rec. 709 < Rec. 2020
Rec. 2020 < DCI-P3 < Rec. 709
Rec. 709 < Rec. 2020 < DCI-P3
questions.hint: The newer Rec. number (used for UHD) has the widest triangle.
questions.r: Slide 28: the dashed Rec. 709 (HDTV) triangle is innermost, the solid DCI-P3 (cinema) triangle is in the middle, and the dotted Rec. 2020 (UHD) triangle is the widest.
questions.why: diagram with three labelled gamuts

questions.q: Which HDR standard uses static metadata?
o: HDR10+
HDR10
Dolby Vision
SL-HDR1
questions.hint: Static means one set of values for the whole programme. Which format is the oldest and simplest?
questions.r: Slides 32-33: HDR10 uses 10-bit PQ with static metadata. HDR10+ and Dolby Vision use dynamic metadata; SL-HDR1 carries dynamic reconstruction data.
questions.why: repeated in two tables (slides 32 and 33)

questions.q: Which HDR standard uses Hybrid Log-Gamma signal encoding and requires no HDR metadata?
o: HDR10
HLG
HDR10+
Dolby Vision
questions.hint: Find the table row whose metadata cell says neither 'static' nor 'dynamic'.
questions.r: Slide 32: HLG = Hybrid Log-Gamma, 10/12-bit, no HDR metadata required, needs a compatible display chain. HDR10 and HDR10+ use PQ encoding with metadata.
questions.why: HDR standards table row

questions.q: Which statement about HDR10+ is TRUE according to the HDR standards table?
o: It uses Hybrid Log-Gamma and needs no metadata
It sends an SDR base plus HDR reconstruction data
It uses PQ encoding with static metadata only
It uses PQ encoding with dynamic metadata
questions.hint: HDR10+ keeps the same signal encoding as HDR10 but changes one column.
questions.r: Slide 32: HDR10+ = 10-bit, PQ, dynamic metadata (scene/frame), SDR conversion required. Static PQ metadata is HDR10; no metadata is HLG; SDR base + reconstruction is SL-HDR1.
questions.why: predicted variant: sibling rows of the same table as distractors

questions.q: In the family of DVB standards, DVB-CA stands for:
o: Common interface for Conditional Access
Cable Access transmission system
Channel Allocation specification
Compression Algorithm for audio and video
questions.hint: Think of the slot in a set-top box where a pay-TV smart card module goes.
questions.r: Slide 35: DVB-CA = common interface for conditional access. Cable transmission is DVB-C, service information is DVB-SI, and return channels are DVB-RC.
questions.why: acronym list; acronym questions appear in past exams

questions.q: What is the correct order of processing blocks in the DVB-S transmitter (ETS 300 421)?
o: Outer coding, scrambling, inner coding, interleaving, QPSK modulation, baseband shaping
Scrambling, outer coding, interleaving, inner coding, baseband shaping, QPSK modulation
Scrambling, inner coding, interleaving, outer coding, baseband shaping, QPSK modulation
Interleaving, scrambling, outer coding, inner coding, QPSK modulation, baseband shaping
questions.hint: Randomize first, then the outer code, shuffle, the inner code, shape the pulses, and modulate last.
questions.r: Slide 38 and Blocks 1-6: scrambling, outer coding (Reed-Solomon), interleaving, inner coding (convolutional), baseband shaping, QPSK modulation. The outer code comes before the inner code, and modulation is always last.
questions.why: block diagram that structures the whole last part of the lecture (Blocks 1-6)

questions.q: The main purpose of data randomization (scrambling) in DVB-S is to:
o: encrypt pay-TV programs so only subscribers can watch them
add redundancy so up to 8 byte errors per packet can be corrected
disperse signal energy to avoid an unmodulated carrier
spread burst errors so the decoder sees only isolated errors
questions.hint: Long runs of identical bits make the signal look like a plain carrier. What does randomizing the bits do to the energy?
questions.r: Slide 39: packets are randomized to disperse the signal energy and prevent the emission of an apparently unmodulated carrier (modulo-2 addition of a 1503-byte pseudo-random sequence). It is not encryption (that is conditional access); spreading burst errors is interleaving.
questions.why: Block 1 definition; 'scrambling vs encryption' is a classic trap

questions.q: The outer code used in DVB-S is the truncated Reed-Solomon code:
questions.hint: The first number is the packet length after coding; the second is the MPEG-2 packet length.
questions.r: Slide 40: RS(204, 188, 8) turns a 188-byte packet into a 204-byte packet and corrects up to 8 errors. RS(188, 204, 8) swaps the lengths; 16 is the number of added bytes, not the number of correctable errors.
questions.why: Block 2 code name with exact numbers

questions.q: The interleaver in the DVB-S chain is used mainly to:
o: reduce the bit rate by removing redundant information
disperse signal energy to avoid an unmodulated carrier
shape the pulse edges of the signal before modulation
help correct burst errors missed by inner decoding
questions.hint: Recall the 'TRANSMITTED-DATA' example: one long block of errors became a few isolated errors.
questions.r: Slide 42: a convolutional interleaver improves the ability to correct a large number of burst errors missed by the inner decoding; after deinterleaving, a burst becomes scattered single errors. Energy dispersal is scrambling; pulse shaping is Block 5.
questions.why: Block 3 definition plus three example slides (44-46)

questions.q: The inner code in the DVB-S chain is:
o: a Reed–Solomon block code
a convolutional code
a Huffman code
a run-length code
questions.hint: The outer code is the Reed–Solomon one.
questions.r: Slide 46: the inner code is convolutional (basic rate 1/2) and can be punctured to higher rates. Reed–Solomon is the outer code; Huffman and run-length coding compress data rather than protect it.
questions.why: Block 4 with exact parameters

questions.q: In Block 5 (baseband pulse shaping), the data stream is coded with Gray code because:
o: its code words differ in only one place
it doubles the number of bits per symbol
it encrypts the stream for conditional access
it adds parity bytes for error correction
questions.hint: Neighbouring states should differ as little as possible, so a small error changes few bits.
questions.r: Slide 46: Gray code means individual code words differ only in one place; the signal is then filtered so that the pulse edges are shaped before modulation. Parity bytes come from the RS outer code.
questions.why: definition given in parentheses on slide

questions.q: In QPSK modulation as used in DVB-S, each carrier phase state represents:
o: a single bit
a pair of bits
three bits
one byte
questions.hint: 'Quadrature' means four states. How many bits are needed to label four states?
questions.r: Slide 49: carrier modulation occurs for individual pairs of bits (x1, x2). Four phases (π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4) give 2 bits per symbol, because 2^2 = 4.
questions.why: Block 6 core idea; appears on slides 49-52

questions.q: The ITU-R 601 Recommendation defines:
o: how television signals are sampled digitally
how digital video is compressed for broadcast TV
how satellite television is modulated
which colours UHD screens can show
questions.hint: It gives two sampling rates.
questions.r: Slide 15: ITU-R 601 sets the sampling of luminance and chrominance so that 625- and 525-line systems are compatible. Compression is MPEG, modulation is DVB, gamut is Rec. 2020.

questions.q: A Single Frequency Network (SFN) is one in which:
o: all transmitters use one frequency
each transmitter sends the same signal on its own frequency
one satellite transponder serves a whole country
each frequency carries exactly one programme
questions.hint: Read the name word by word.
questions.r: Slide 22 compares SFN support: DVB-T and ISDB-T yes, ATSC no. In an SFN every transmitter uses the same frequency for the same signal.

questions.q: The DVB project is:
o: an industry-led consortium that designs open TV standards
a European government agency that assigns TV frequencies
a video compression method used for satellite TV
a satellite operator that broadcasts digital TV
questions.hint: About 250 members work together.
questions.r: Slide 34: DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting) is an industry-led consortium that designs open technical standards for digital television and data services.

questions.q: DVB-T is the DVB standard for:
o: terrestrial transmission
transmission by satellite
cable transmission
return channels
questions.hint: T for what is on the ground.
questions.r: Slide 35: DVB-S satellite, DVB-C cable, DVB-T terrestrial, DVB-RC return channels.

questions.q: In a digital TV receiver, the demultiplexer:
o: splits video, audio and data
selects the wanted channel from the antenna
converts the digital picture to analog
expands the compressed picture again
questions.hint: One stream goes in, several come out.
questions.r: Slide 36: tuner, demodulator, demultiplexer, then decompression and D/A conversion. The demultiplexer splits the stream into video, audio and service data.

questions.q: The Reed–Solomon outer code protects the data by:
o: adding parity bytes that allow error correction
sending every data packet a second time
spreading neighbouring bytes further apart in time
mixing the data with a random sequence
questions.hint: The packet gets longer.
questions.r: Slide 40: 188 bytes become 204; the added bytes allow up to 8 errors to be corrected. Spreading bytes is interleaving, mixing with a random sequence is scrambling.

questions.q: Puncturing a convolutional code:
o: raises the code rate by leaving out coded bits
lowers the code rate by adding parity bits
spreads long burst errors over several packets
maps pairs of bits to carrier phases
questions.hint: Something is removed.
questions.r: Slide 46: the basic rate 1/2 can be increased by puncturing to 2/3, 3/4, 5/6 or 7/8, at the price of weaker protection.

questions.q: Modulation is:
o: applying the transmitted signal to a carrier wave
removing the carrier wave from the received signal
adding parity bytes to the transmitted signal
selecting one channel with a bandpass filter
questions.hint: It happens in the transmitter.
questions.r: Slide 47: modulation applies the transmitted signal s(t) to the carrier wave. Recovering s(t) is demodulation.

questions.q: In frequency modulation (FM), the transmitted signal changes:
o: the carrier's frequency
the carrier's amplitude
the carrier's phase
the carrier's bandwidth
questions.hint: Look at the name.
questions.r: Slide 47: AM changes the amplitude, FM the frequency and PM the phase of the carrier.

questions.q: QPSK stands for:
o: Quadrature Phase Shift Keying
Quantized Pulse Shape Keying
Quick Parallel Signal Keying
Quaternary Power Shift Keying
questions.hint: It shifts the phase of the carrier.
questions.r: Slide 49: QPSK = Quadrature Phase Shift Keying; each of the four phases carries a pair of bits.

questions.q: JPEG stands for:
o: Joint Pictorial Encoding Group
Joint Photographic Expert Group
Japanese Photo Engineering Group
Joint Picture Exchange Guild
questions.hint: The 'J' reflects cooperation between ISO and CCITT; the 'E' refers to people, not to encoding.
questions.r: Slide 2 expands JPEG as Joint Photographic Expert Group (1986), a joint effort of ISO and CCITT. 'Encoding', 'Engineering' and 'Exchange' are invented expansions.
questions.why: bold heading on the Part 4 title slide; acronym questions are common

questions.q: Lossless image compression is a method that:
o: restores the original data on decompression, with nothing permanently lost
removes 'excess' data and decompresses by approximating the original data
discards the high-frequency components that the human eye does not notice
reduces the number of bits per sample of every transform coefficient
questions.hint: Compare the two butterflies on the slide: 'exact' versus 'approximate' reconstruction.
questions.r: Slide 3: lossless decompression restores the original data and no data is permanently modified or lost. Approximating the original is the definition of lossy; dropping high frequencies and cutting bits per sample are lossy JPEG steps.
questions.why: basic bold-italic definition pair on slide 3

questions.q: Which statement about the JPEG algorithm is TRUE?
o: It is a purely lossless method that restores the image byte-for-byte
It has no optional modes, so progressive scanning is impossible
It works directly on RGB values in blocks of 16x16 pixels
It exploits limitations of human eyesight to reach high compression ratios
questions.hint: Ask yourself why JPEG can throw data away without the viewer complaining.
questions.r: Slide 4: JPEG takes advantage of the limitations of human eyesight, is lossy with a selectable quality/compression level, and has optional interlacing and progressive modes. It works on 8x8 blocks of luminance/chrominance data, not 16x16 RGB.
questions.why: three plain bullets on slide 4, easy TRUE/FALSE source

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the 'JPEG insights' listed in the lecture?
o: Useful image content usually changes relatively slowly
In an 8x8 block, pixel intensity usually does not change significantly
High spatial frequency components contain more information than low ones
The eye does not quickly notice the loss of high-frequency components
questions.hint: Which frequencies does the slide link to 'less useful details and noise'?
questions.r: Slide 5 says the opposite: LOWER spatial frequency components contain more information, while high frequencies correspond to less useful details and noise. The other three options are listed insights.
questions.why: core rationale slide; NOT-form is easy to build from it

questions.q: What is the correct order of the JPEG encoder phases?
o: Division into blocks, colour conversion, DCT, zig-zag, quantization, entropy coding
Colour conversion, division into blocks, DCT, quantization, zig-zag, entropy coding
Colour conversion, DCT, division into blocks, quantization, entropy coding, zig-zag
Colour conversion, division into blocks, quantization, DCT, zig-zag, entropy coding
questions.hint: You must transform before you can quantize coefficients, and you need a vector before you entropy-code it.
questions.r: Slide 7: 1 conversion to luminance-chrominance, 2 division into blocks, 3 DCT, 4 quantization of DCT coefficients, 5 zig-zag conversion to a vector, 6 entropy coding. Quantizing before the DCT is wrong because quantization acts on DCT coefficients.
questions.why: numbered list plus block diagram on slide 7; structures the whole lecture

questions.q: Which step of the JPEG encoder is the main source of information loss?
o: Quantization of the DCT coefficients
Calculation of the DCT
Zig-zag conversion of the array to a vector
Huffman entropy coding of the vector
questions.hint: Find the step where values are divided and then rounded to integers.
questions.r: Slide 19: 'Quantization error is the main source of lossy compression (!)'. The DCT is an invertible transform, and zig-zag and Huffman coding only reorder or code the data without loss.
questions.why: bold italic with exclamation mark on slide 19

questions.q: After colour conversion, JPEG divides the Y, U and V arrays into blocks of size:
o: 4 x 4 pixels
8 x 8 pixels
16 x 16 pixels
32 x 32 pixels
questions.hint: It is the block size that produces exactly 64 DCT coefficients.
questions.r: Slide 9: the arrays are divided into macroblocks of size 8 x 8, f(x,y) with x, y = 0..7. That is why the zig-zag vector is 1x64; a 16x16 block would give 256 coefficients.
questions.why: 8x8 is repeated on almost every JPEG slide

questions.q: The DCT in JPEG converts the information in an 8x8 block:
o: from the frequency domain to the spatial domain
from the RGB model to the YCbCr model
from the spatial domain to the frequency domain
from a 2D array to a 1x64 vector
questions.hint: Before the DCT you have pixel positions; after it you have cosine components.
questions.r: Slide 11: the DCT converts a block of 8x8 pixels from the spatial domain to the frequency domain (bold italic). The inverse DCT goes the other way; RGB to YCbCr is phase 1 and array to vector is the zig-zag step.
questions.why: bold italic, repeated on slides 11 and 12

questions.q: In the DCT coefficient matrix F(u,v), the DC component is:
o: F(0,0), while all remaining coefficients are AC components
F(7,7), the coefficient of the highest frequency
the average of all 63 AC components of the block
the last element of the vector after the zig-zag scan
questions.hint: DC = 'direct current': the constant part, zero frequency in both directions.
questions.r: Slide 13: F(0,0) is called the DC component and the remaining values are AC components. F(7,7) is the highest-frequency AC coefficient, and DC is the FIRST element of the zig-zag vector [DC, AC1, ..., AC63].
questions.why: bold DC/AC terms on slide 13, used through the whole coding part

questions.q: In the lecture, quantization of DCT coefficients is described as:
o: conversion of the coefficient array into a vector
coding the difference between DC values of adjacent blocks
replacing fixed-length symbols with variable-length codewords
reduction of the number of bits per sample
questions.hint: Remember the 6-bit example where 45 became 44 and then 40.
questions.r: Slide 19: quantization is the 'reduction the number of bits per sample'; the more bits truncated, the more precision lost. The other options describe zig-zag, DPCM and entropy coding.
questions.why: headline definition on slide 19; siblings make good distractors

questions.q: In JPEG quantization, each DCT coefficient is:
o: multiplied by its table value and rounded
reduced by its table value and rounded
divided by its table value and rounded
replaced by its table value and sorted
questions.hint: A larger table value should make the stored number smaller.
questions.r: Slide 20: the coefficient is divided by the quantization-table value and rounded to an integer. Multiplying by the table value is the decoding step.
questions.why: formula box on slide 20

questions.q: What is the difference between uniform and non-uniform quantization in JPEG?
o: Uniform uses quantization tables; non-uniform uses a single constant Q
Uniform applies only to luminance; non-uniform applies only to chrominance
Uniform rounds coefficients down; non-uniform rounds coefficients up
Uniform uses one constant Q(u,v); non-uniform uses quantization tables
questions.hint: 'Uniform' means the same step for every coefficient.
questions.r: Slide 20: uniform quantization -> Q(u,v) is a constant; non-uniform quantization -> quantization tables are used. The first option reverses the two.
questions.why: bold italic pair on slide 20; easy to reverse

questions.q: Which statement about JPEG quantization tables is TRUE?
o: The standard defines one default table, shared by the Y, U and V components alike; none go in the header
The standard defines two default tables, for luminance and chrominance; custom ones may go in the header
The standard defines three default tables, one each for the R, G and B components
The standard forbids custom tables in the header, so only the two default tables may ever be used
questions.hint: How many kinds of component exist after the colour conversion?
questions.r: Slide 21: custom quantization tables can be included in the image header, and the standard defines two default tables, one for luminance and one for chrominance. Quantization happens after RGB is converted, so there are no R/G/B tables.
questions.why: two bullets plus both tables on slide 21

questions.q: Why do the values of a JPEG quantization table grow toward the high frequencies?
o: High frequencies are quantized more coarsely, because the eye is less sensitive to them
Low frequencies are quantized more coarsely, because they mostly carry image noise
High frequencies are stored with more bits, because they hold the most useful detail
High frequencies are never sent, because the decoder can compute them from the DC value
questions.hint: Larger divisor means a smaller quantized number and less precision. Where does the eye care least?
questions.r: Slides 20–21: the eye is most sensitive to low frequencies (upper left) and less to high ones (lower right), so the table values grow toward the lower right and remove detail there first.
questions.why: combines slides 20 and 21; numeric-interpretation style

questions.q: The zig-zag algorithm in JPEG:
o: maps a 1x64 vector back into an 8x8 matrix ordered by frequency
sorts the 64 coefficients by magnitude in descending order
maps an 8x8 matrix to a 1x64 vector, putting low frequencies first
maps an 8x8 matrix to a 1x63 vector, dropping the DC coefficient
questions.hint: Low frequencies sit in the upper-left corner, and the scan starts there.
questions.r: Slide 25: zig-zag maps an 8x8 matrix to a 1x64 vector, grouping low-frequency coefficients at the top of the vector and high ones at the bottom. DC stays as the first element: [DC, AC1, ..., AC63].
questions.why: two bullets plus diagram on slides 25-26

questions.q: The zig-zag algorithm used in JPEG was proposed by:
o: D. A. Huffman in 1952
A. Lempel and J. Ziv in 1977
the Joint Photographic Expert Group in 1986
A. G. Tescher in 1978
questions.hint: The name appears on slide 25 in brackets, with a year from the late 1970s.
questions.r: Slide 25: Zig-Zag algorithm (A. G. Tescher 1978). Huffman coding is used in phase 6, LZ77 appears only in WebP lossless mode, and 1986 is when the JPEG group was formed.
questions.why: named person and year on the slide; 'was created by' questions are common

questions.q: DPCM, used for coding DC coefficients in JPEG, stands for:
o: Discrete Pixel Cosine Mapping
Differential Pulse Code Modulation
Differential Prediction Coding Matrix
Dynamic Pulse Compression Method
questions.hint: It codes differences, and the rest of the name comes from classic telephony signal coding.
questions.r: Slide 29: Differential Pulse Code Modulation codes the difference between the DC of the current and the previous 8x8 block. The other expansions are invented.
questions.why: bold acronym with italic expansion on slide 29

questions.q: In the JPEG entropy coding stage, DC and AC coefficients are coded respectively with:
o: RLE for DC and DPCM for AC
Huffman coding for DC, AC left uncoded
DPCM for DC and RLE for AC
DPCM for both DC and AC values
questions.hint: Which coefficient is large and similar in neighbouring blocks, and which ones are mostly zeros?
questions.r: Slides 7, 28 and 35: DC uses DPCM because DC values of neighbouring blocks are close, and AC uses run-length encoding because the 1x64 vectors contain many zeros. Both results are then Huffman-coded.
questions.why: DPCM/RLC boxes in the slide 7 diagram plus section titles 6.1 (DC) and (AC)

questions.q: In run-length encoding of JPEG AC coefficients, a pair (skip, value) means:
o: skip = number of zeros, value = the next non-zero coefficient; (0,0) ends the block
skip = number of non-zero coefficients, value = the count of zeros that follow them
skip = index of the block, value = its DC coefficient after DPCM coding
skip = number of zeros, value = their position; (0,0) starts a run of 16 zeros
questions.hint: First say how many zeros you jump over, then say what you land on.
questions.r: Slide 36: skip is the number of zeros, value is the next non-zero component, and the pair (0,0) indicates the end of the block. Example: 0,0,0,0,0,1 -> (5,1). A run of 16 zeros is ZRL, not (0,0).
questions.why: bold italic definitions plus diagram on slide 36

questions.q: JPEG XR is:
o: a Microsoft technology introduced in 2006 as Windows Media Photo and standardized in 2009
a Google web format introduced in 2010 whose lossy mode is based on VP8 prediction
a format by Fabrice Bellard from 2014 based on a subset of the HEVC (H.265) standard
an MPEG container standard from 2015 built on the ISO Base Media File Format
questions.hint: Think of the 'Windows' world and its HD Photo precursor.
questions.r: Slide 48: JPEG XR was introduced in 2006 as Windows Media Photo (followed by HD Photo) and standardized in 2009 as ISO/IEC 29199 and ITU-T T.832. The other options describe WebP, BPG and HEIF.
questions.why: sibling-format distractors, the 'X is:' style

questions.q: WebP lossy compression is based on:
o: a subset of HEVC (H.265), stored in a .bpg file
an integer-based lapped transform in a TIFF-based structure
VP8 intra-frame prediction, stored in a RIFF container
MANIAC adaptive arithmetic coding with context trees
questions.hint: WebP borrows its lossy mode from a Google video codec.
questions.r: Slide 49: WebP lossy mode uses VP8 intra-frame prediction in a RIFF container; lossless mode combines transforms, LZ77 and entropy coding. HEVC is BPG, the lapped transform is JPEG XR, and MANIAC is FLIF.
questions.why: compression row of the WebP slide; sibling formats as distractors

questions.q: BPG stands for:
o: Binary Portable Graphics, introduced by Google in 2010
Better Progressive Graphics, introduced by Microsoft in 2006
Basic Portable Graphics, introduced by the JPEG committee in 2021
Better Portable Graphics, introduced by Fabrice Bellard in 2014
questions.hint: It aims to be 'better' than JPEG and was made by one well-known programmer, not a company.
questions.r: Slide 50: BPG (Better Portable Graphics) was introduced in December 2014 by Fabrice Bellard and is based on a subset of HEVC (H.265). Google 2010 is WebP, Microsoft 2006 is JPEG XR, and 2021 is JPEG XL.
questions.why: acronym expanded in the slide title, plus author and date

questions.q: Which statement about HEIF is TRUE?
o: It is an MPEG container (ISO/IEC 23008-12) on ISOBMFF that separates image storage from coding
It is a codec that always compresses images with Google's VP8 intra-frame prediction method
It was developed by Jon Sneyers and Pieter Wuille for exact, lossless image preservation
It is a Microsoft format that uses a TIFF-based structure and an integer lapped transform
questions.hint: HEIF is a 'file format' (a container), not a codec; HEIC is what commonly sits inside.
questions.r: Slide 51: HEIF is the MPEG container standard ISO/IEC 23008-12 built on ISOBMFF; the selected codec (commonly HEVC, as in HEIC) determines compression. Apple adopted it in 2017 (iOS 11, macOS High Sierra). The other options describe WebP, FLIF and JPEG XR.
questions.why: origin and distinctive rows of the HEIF slide

questions.q: FLIF (Free Lossless Image Format) codes images using:
o: VarDCT and modular coding defined in ISO/IEC 18181
MANIAC, an adaptive arithmetic coder with context trees
VP8 intra-frame prediction with a lossless alpha channel
HEVC coding tools with a compact header over the stream
questions.hint: The method's name sounds like a word for a wild, crazy person.
questions.r: Slide 52: FLIF (Jon Sneyers and Pieter Wuille, 2015) uses MANIAC, an adaptive arithmetic coder with image-specific context trees. Its development stopped and its ideas continued via FUIF into JPEG XL, which is the VarDCT/modular option.
questions.why: detail row on the FLIF slide

questions.q: Which feature is distinctive of JPEG XL?
o: Apple added it to iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra in 2017
Web use needs a JavaScript decoder and HEVC patents may apply
Existing JPEG files can be recompressed losslessly and restored byte-for-byte
Lossless coding and transparency arrived after the initial lossy release
questions.hint: It is the newest JPEG-committee format and is designed to be friendly to the huge legacy of old .jpg files.
questions.r: Slide 53: JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181, 2021, reference library libjxl) lets existing JPEG files be recompressed without loss and later restored byte-for-byte. The distractors are the 'distinctive' rows of HEIF, BPG and WebP.
questions.why: 'Distinctive' row; sibling formats' distinctive rows as distractors

questions.q: The more bits quantization cuts from each coefficient:
o: the more precision is lost
the larger the file gets
the sharper the edges look
the more colours are kept
questions.hint: Less data, less detail.
questions.r: Slide 19: the more bits we truncate, the more precision we lose. Quantization error is the main source of loss.

questions.q: During JPEG decoding, dequantization:
o: multiplies by the table values, but the rounding loss remains
divides by the table values, which restores the exact original
removes the block borders that appeared during encoding
adds back the rounding errors stored in the file header
questions.hint: Rounding cannot be undone.
questions.r: Slide 23: the decoder multiplies each coefficient by its table value and applies the inverse DCT; the result is close to the original, not exact.

questions.q: A two-dimensional DCT of a block is computed as:
o: 1-D transforms of the rows, then of the columns
one long 1-D transform of the whole zig-zag vector
a 3-D transform of the Y, U and V planes
the average of all row and column sums
questions.hint: Two passes over the same block.
questions.r: Slide 13: two series of one-dimensional transforms, first the rows and then the columns.

questions.q: Why is a chessboard pattern hard for JPEG?
o: It has strong high-frequency coefficients
It has only one DC coefficient
It has no luminance information
It does not fit into blocks of 8 × 8 pixels
questions.hint: JPEG removes high frequencies first.
questions.r: Slide 16: the DCT of the chessboard has large coefficients in the high-frequency corner, exactly where JPEG quantizes most coarsely.

questions.q: Why does the zig-zag order help run-length coding?
o: It groups the many zeros at the end of the vector
It removes all of the zeros before they are coded
It sorts the coefficients from large to small
It makes every coefficient an even number
questions.hint: Where do the high frequencies end up?
questions.r: Slides 25 and 36: low frequencies come first, so the vectors have many zeros, especially at the end.

questions.q: Why does DPCM suit the DC coefficients?
o: Neighbouring blocks have similar values
Most of the DC values in an image are zero
DC values are always the smallest values
DC values change sign from block to block
questions.hint: Differences should be small.
questions.r: Slide 29: the DC value is large but often close to that of the previous block, so the difference is small and needs fewer bits.

questions.q: Entropy coding compresses data by replacing:
o: fixed-length symbols with variable-length codewords
variable-length symbols with fixed-length codewords
large coefficients with small rounded ones
several similar blocks with one average block
questions.hint: Frequent symbols become short.
questions.r: Slide 27: the entropy coder replaces each fixed-length input symbol by a variable-length prefix codeword. Rounding is quantization and is lossy.

questions.q: In JPEG, the EOB code means that:
o: only zeros remain in the block
the whole image has ended
a run of exactly 16 zeros follows
the next block is empty
questions.hint: B stands for block.
questions.r: Slide 40: EOB (end of block) = zeros to the end of the block. A run of 16 zeros has its own code, ZRL.

questions.q: According to the lecture's JPEG pipeline, which two steps actually discard information?
o: DCT and zig-zag scan
Chroma subsampling and quantization
Colour transform and entropy coding
Quantization and entropy coding
questions.hint: Two red boxes in the seven-step pipeline: one thins out colour, the other divides and rounds.
