questions.r: Slide 6 marks only chroma subsampling and quantization as LOSSY, with quantization as the main one. The DCT is invertible and entropy coding is lossless, so the options containing them are wrong.
questions.why: LOSSY labels on pipeline slide + summary slide + review question on slide 62

questions.q: Which statement about the DCT step in JPEG is TRUE?
o: The DCT itself is invertible; the loss comes from rounding after division by Q(u,v)
The DCT is the main lossy step because it throws away the high-frequency coefficients
The DCT converts RGB into YCbCr before the image is split into 8×8 blocks
The DCT outputs 64 DC coefficients, one for each pixel of the 8×8 block
questions.hint: Ask yourself: could you get the pixels back exactly from the 64 coefficients before anything is rounded?
questions.r: Slide 8: 'the DCT is invertible - the loss comes from rounding after the division'. Throwing away high frequencies happens in quantization, not in the DCT; RGB->YCbCr is the colour transform.
questions.why: explicit bullet + review question 'which JPEG step introduces the loss'

questions.q: Lowering the JPEG quality factor has which effect?
o: Smaller Q values, fewer zeros, a smaller file with sharper edges
Larger Q values, fewer zeros, a larger file with visible blocking
Unchanged Q values, but stronger chroma subsampling
Larger Q values, more zeros, a smaller file with visible blocking
questions.hint: The quality factor scales the divisor. Dividing by a bigger number and rounding produces what more often?
questions.r: Slide 8: lower quality -> larger Q -> more zeros -> smaller file, visible blocking. Smaller Q would keep more detail and give a larger file.
questions.why: arrow chain on DCT/quantization slide; links to quality test on slide 9

questions.q: 4:2:0 chroma subsampling means that colour is stored at:
o: half resolution horizontally and vertically
half resolution horizontally only
a quarter of the resolution horizontally only
full resolution, but with fewer bits
questions.hint: Both directions are affected.
questions.r: Slide 7: 4:2:0 halves the colour resolution in both directions, which makes the whole image about 50 % smaller. 4:2:2 halves it horizontally only; 4:1:1 quarters it horizontally.
questions.why: table of values; 4:2:0 named the most common choice in JPEG

questions.q: Which set lists exactly the four modes defined by the JPEG standard?
o: Baseline, extended, wavelet, lossless
Sequential, interlaced, predictive, fractal
Progressive, hierarchical, near-lossless, layered
Sequential, progressive, lossless, hierarchical
questions.hint: One pass; several scans; an exact copy; a pyramid of resolutions.
questions.r: Slides 10-11: one standard, four modes - sequential, progressive, lossless and hierarchical. Wavelets belong to JPEG 2000, not to the original JPEG modes.
questions.why: agenda item + tree diagram + dedicated 'four modes' slide

questions.q: According to the lecture, almost all real JPEG files use which combination?
o: Sequential mode, Huffman coding, 8-bit samples
Progressive mode, arithmetic coding, 12-bit samples
Sequential mode, arithmetic coding, 12-bit samples
Hierarchical mode, Huffman coding, 8-bit samples
questions.hint: Arithmetic coding and 12-bit depth are 'in the standard but rarely supported'.
questions.r: Slide 10: 'In practice: almost all files are sequential + Huffman + 8-bit'. Arithmetic coding and 12-bit depth exist in the standard but are rarely supported.
questions.why: 'In practice' highlight box

questions.q: Which statement about the JPEG sequential (baseline) mode is TRUE?
o: It codes the image in several scans that gradually add detail
Every JPEG decoder must implement baseline mode
It replaces the DCT and quantization with pixel prediction
It allows only arithmetic coding as the entropy coder
questions.hint: Think of the one mode that every image viewer is guaranteed to open.
questions.r: Slide 12: baseline must be implemented in every decoder; single pass, left to right, top to bottom; Huffman or arithmetic coding. Multi-scan refinement is progressive mode and prediction is lossless mode.
questions.why: bold 'baseline' bullet; sibling-mode distractors

questions.q: The two algorithms available in JPEG progressive mode are:
o: Spectral selection and DPCM
Pyramid coding and wavelet decomposition
Spectral selection and successive approximation
Successive approximation and LZW dictionary coding
questions.hint: One splits the data by frequency band, the other by bit precision; the slide says they can be combined.
questions.r: Slide 14: progressive mode uses spectral selection and successive approximation, and a combination of both is possible. DPCM belongs to lossless/DC coding and pyramids to hierarchical mode.
questions.why: bold italic terms + red note 'possible a combination of both'

questions.q: Successive approximation in progressive JPEG means:
o: Sending the lower-frequency DCT bands first, then the higher ones
Sending all DCT coefficients a few bits at a time, MSB first
Sending a low-resolution frame first, then up-sampled refinements
Predicting each pixel from its left and upper neighbours
questions.hint: Approximation = precision. Picture each 8-bit value being revealed bit-plane by bit-plane.
questions.r: Slide 16: all DCT components are sent a few bits at a time, e.g. first run p1 = 4 bits from the MSB, next run p2 = 1 bit. Sending low-frequency bands first is spectral selection (slide 15).
questions.why: sibling-term definitions (spectral selection vs successive approximation vs hierarchical)

questions.q: JPEG hierarchical mode is best described as:
o: A single-pass mode coding the blocks left to right, top to bottom
A multi-pass mode sending parts of the quantized DCT data of one resolution
A predictive mode without DCT that restores every pixel exactly
A 'super-progressive' mode coding a pyramid of resolutions
questions.hint: Think of a stack of frames of growing size, like a thumbnail growing into the full picture.
questions.r: Slide 23: hierarchical mode supports multiple resolutions; the image is split into frames, the lowest resolution is coded first, and each up-sampled result becomes the prediction for the next phase. Multi-pass at one resolution is progressive mode.
questions.why: dedicated slide; definition with sibling-mode distractors

questions.q: Lossless JPEG reconstructs every pixel exactly because it:
o: Uses a quantization table with all Q values equal to 1
Applies the DCT with 12-bit precision instead of 8-bit
Replaces the DCT and quantization with prediction
Skips chroma subsampling but keeps the DCT and quantization
questions.hint: Remove the two sources of irreversible loss and code only what is left over.
questions.r: Slide 18: lossless mode is predictive coding with no DCT and no quantization; only the prediction error X - P is entropy-coded. Keeping DCT + quantization would still involve rounding.
questions.why: 'No DCT, no quantization' box + slide 11 note

questions.q: Lossless JPEG predicts each pixel from:
o: its left, upper and upper-left neighbours
the average value of its whole 8 × 8 block
the same pixel of the previous image
the low-frequency DCT coefficients
questions.hint: Only pixels that are already decoded can be used.
questions.r: Slide 21: the predictors combine A (left), B (above) and C (upper-left). Lossless JPEG has no DCT, and there is no previous image.
questions.why: predictor table + worked example + solution slide

questions.q: A Huffman code can be decoded unambiguously because:
o: All codewords have the same length
The decoder rebuilds the dictionary on the fly
No codeword is a prefix of any other codeword
Each message is mapped to one sub-interval of [0, 1)
questions.hint: Symbols sit only at the leaves of the tree, never on the path to another symbol.
questions.r: Slide 25: Huffman generates a prefix-free code, which allows unambiguous decoding. Rebuilding a dictionary describes LZW, and a sub-interval of [0, 1) describes arithmetic coding.
questions.why: bullet on slide 25 + review question 'why is a Huffman code prefix-free' (slide 62)

questions.q: In each step of building a Huffman tree, the algorithm:
o: Merges the two nodes with the lowest frequencies under a new node
Merges the two nodes with the highest frequencies under a new node
Splits the symbol set into two halves of equal total probability
Gives the shortest codeword to the least frequent symbol
questions.hint: Slide title: 'repeatedly merge the two ___ symbols'. Rare symbols should end up deep in the tree.
questions.r: Slide 26: while more than one tree remains, take the two lowest and add them under a new root (first merge: H:1 + D:2 = 3). Frequent symbols get short codes, so the rarest are merged first.
questions.why: slide title + 12-step worked example

questions.q: The entropy of a source is:
o: the length of its longest codeword
the lower bound on its average code length
the total number of different symbols it uses
the size of its fixed-length code
questions.hint: No symbol-by-symbol code can beat it.
questions.r: Slide 24: entropy H is the lower bound on the average code length in bits per symbol. A Huffman code always stays within one bit of it.
questions.why: rule box with formula; predicted numeric variant

questions.q: The compression factor compares:
o: the data size before and after compression
the image quality before and after compression
the encoding time with the decoding time
the number of symbols with the number of codes
questions.hint: It is a ratio of two sizes.
questions.r: Slide 42: compression factor = size before / size after. It says nothing about quality or speed.
questions.why: formula box + learning outcome 'compute the compression factor by hand'

questions.q: Which statement comparing arithmetic coding with Huffman coding is TRUE?
o: Huffman can spend less than one bit on a symbol whose probability is 0.99, unlike arithmetic coding
Arithmetic coding assigns its own separate codeword to each single symbol
Arithmetic coding maps the whole message to one number and allows fractional bits per symbol
Arithmetic coding is lossy, whereas Huffman coding is a lossless method that keeps every bit
questions.hint: Huffman: one codeword per symbol, in whole bits. What does arithmetic coding output for the whole message?
questions.r: Slide 45: Huffman costs a whole number of bits (at least 1) per symbol even if p = 0.99; arithmetic coding gives one number for the whole message and can approach the entropy with fractional bits. Both are lossless (slide 61).
questions.why: comparison slide + review question 'when does arithmetic beat Huffman'

questions.q: The lecture attributes arithmetic coding to:
o: David Huffman, 1952
Peter Elias, 1960s
Terry Welch, 1984
Gregory Wallace, 1991
questions.hint: Not the author of the tree-based code, and not the author of the JPEG paper in the references.
questions.r: Slide 46: author - Peter Elias (1960s). David Huffman (1952) invented Huffman coding, G. K. Wallace wrote the 1991 JPEG paper and Welch is the W in LZW.
questions.why: author with photo on slide; 'created by' questions are common

questions.q: GIF stands for:
o: Graphical Information Format
General Image Format
Graphics Interchange Format
Graphics Indexed Format
questions.hint: It was made for exchanging pictures between users over modems.
questions.r: Slide 56: GIF = Graphics Interchange Format (versions GIF87a and GIF89a). The other expansions are invented.
questions.why: bold italic expansion on slide

questions.q: Which statement about GIF is TRUE?
o: It was developed by Unisys and CompuServe for sending images via modems
It was developed by Aldus Corp. in the 1980s and was later supported by Microsoft
It uses DEFLATE compression and supports 24-bit TrueColor images
It supports an alpha channel with variable transparency and gamma correction
questions.hint: Think of the dial-up era and its online services.
questions.r: Slide 56: GIF was developed by UNISYS Corp. and CompuServe for modem transmission, uses LZW, supports 8-bit images only, and GIF89a adds simple animation. Aldus/Microsoft is TIFF; DEFLATE, variable alpha and gamma are PNG.
questions.why: sibling-format attributes as distractors

questions.q: Because GIF supports 8-bit images only, the maximum number of colours in one GIF image is:
o: 16.7 million
questions.hint: 2 raised to the number of bits per pixel.
questions.r: 2^8 = 256 colours (slide 60: 'lossless (LZW), 256 colours'). 65 536 = 2^16 and 16.7 million = 2^24 (TrueColor).
questions.why: comparison table + 'supports 8-bit images only' on slide 56

questions.q: Which statement about TIFF is TRUE according to the lecture?
o: It is lossless unless the JPEG tag is used, and it was developed by Aldus Corp.
It was designed to replace GIF and adds gamma correction and 2-D interlacing
It supports only 8-bit palette images and simple animation in its 89a version
It is based on AV1 intra-frame coding and supports HDR and wide colour gamut
questions.hint: T = Tagged; one particular tag switches on lossy compression.
questions.r: Slide 57: TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) stores many image types, was developed by Aldus Corp. in the 1980s (later supported by Microsoft) and is lossless when not using the JPEG tag. Replacing GIF describes PNG; 89a describes GIF; AV1 describes AVIF.
questions.why: TIFF slide; bold 'lossless'

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of PNG over GIF?
o: Alpha channel (variable transparency)
Gamma correction
Two-dimensional interlacing
Support for animation
questions.hint: The PNG slide lists exactly one disadvantage.
questions.r: Slide 58: the advantages are alpha channel, gamma correction, 2-D interlacing (GIF uses 1-D) and 5-25% better compression; the disadvantage is that PNG does not support animation (only via the APNG extension, slide 60).
questions.why: advantages/disadvantage list; NOT-form

questions.q: Which pairing of dictionary method and file format is correct?
o: LZW in PNG; DEFLATE (LZ77 + arithmetic coding) in GIF
LZW in GIF and TIFF; DEFLATE (LZ77 + Huffman) in PNG
LZW in PNG and ZIP; DEFLATE (LZ78 + Huffman) in TIFF
LZW in JPEG; DEFLATE (DCT + Huffman) in PNG and GIF
questions.hint: The lecture's link: PNG = prediction + LZ77 + Huffman. The older palette format uses the Lempel-Ziv-Welch method.
questions.r: Slide 55: LZW (GIF, TIFF) builds its dictionary on the fly and does not transmit it; DEFLATE (PNG, ZIP, gzip) = LZ77 back-references + Huffman coding. PNG also applies row filters (Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) before DEFLATE.
questions.why: LZW/DEFLATE slide + 'Connection with this lecture' bullet

questions.q: According to the format comparison table, which set contains only formats that support animation?
o: GIF, PNG, TIFF
JPEG, WebP, AVIF
GIF, WebP, AVIF
PNG, GIF, JPEG
questions.hint: PNG needs an extension (APNG) for this; JPEG and TIFF say 'no'.
questions.r: Slide 60: animation = yes for GIF, WebP and AVIF; PNG = no (APNG ext.), JPEG = no, TIFF = no.
questions.why: comparison table; classify-style question

questions.q: WebP (Google, 2010) is:
o: Based on AV1 intra-frame coding, with HDR and wide gamut, often smaller but slower to encode
Wavelet-based with no 8×8 blocking, offering resolution scalability for digital cinema
Lossless only, using DEFLATE after Sub, Up, Average and Paeth row filters
VP8-based, lossy and lossless, with alpha and animation, about 25-35% smaller than JPEG
questions.hint: Google built it to beat JPEG on the web while also covering what GIF and PNG are used for.
questions.r: Slide 59: WebP = lossy (VP8-based) and lossless mode, alpha channel, animation, typically 25-35% smaller than JPEG at similar quality. AV1-based is AVIF; wavelets are JPEG 2000; DEFLATE with row filters is PNG.
questions.why: modern web formats slide + comparison table

questions.q: Which JPEG successor can recompress existing JPEG files losslessly (about 20% smaller)?
o: JPEG-LS
JPEG 2000
JPEG AI
JPEG XL
questions.hint: The one whose decoding came back in Chrome 155 (Oct 2026).
questions.r: Slide 54: JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181) recompresses existing JPEGs losslessly (~20% smaller), supports HDR and animation, and is 30-50% smaller than JPEG at equal quality. JPEG-LS is prediction-based lossless (LOCO-I), JPEG 2000 uses wavelets, JPEG AI uses learned coding.
questions.why: 'NEW' badge + successors slide + slide 59

questions.q: According to the lecture summary, which format choice is correct?
o: Photos -> JPEG/WebP/AVIF; graphics and screenshots -> PNG; simple animations -> GIF/WebP
Photos -> PNG/GIF; graphics and screenshots -> JPEG; simple animations -> TIFF/PNG
Photos -> GIF/TIFF; graphics and screenshots -> AVIF; simple animations -> PNG/JPEG
Photos -> TIFF/PNG; graphics and screenshots -> WebP; simple animations -> JPEG/PNG
questions.hint: Lossy for photos, lossless with sharp edges for screenshots, and only formats that can animate for the last case.
questions.r: Slide 61: photos -> JPEG/WebP/AVIF, graphics and screenshots -> PNG, simple animations -> GIF/WebP. PNG and JPEG have no animation (slide 60).
questions.why: summary slide 'three things to remember'

questions.q: What does lossless JPEG store for each pixel?
o: the prediction error
the quantized DCT value
the block average
the original value
questions.hint: Actual minus predicted.
questions.r: Slide 19: only the difference between the pixel and its prediction is entropy-coded. There is no DCT and no quantization.

questions.q: In a Huffman code, the most frequent symbols get:
o: short codewords
the longest codewords
codewords of equal length
two codewords each
questions.hint: Save bits where it counts.
questions.r: Slides 25–26: frequent symbols lie near the root of the tree and get short codes; rare symbols get long ones.

questions.q: In arithmetic coding, a more probable message gets:
o: a wider interval and fewer bits
a wider interval and more bits
a narrower interval and fewer bits
a narrower interval and more bits
questions.hint: A wide interval is easy to point at.
questions.r: Slide 45: the more probable the message, the wider its interval and the fewer bits are needed to name a number inside it.

questions.q: How does an arithmetic decoder know where the message ends?
o: from a stop character or the symbol count
from the first codeword that repeats
from the width of the first interval
from a marker inside the quantization table
questions.hint: Two solutions are on the slide.
questions.r: Slide 52: the encoder adds a stop character (preferred) or sends the number of coded symbols.

questions.q: JPEG 2000 differs from baseline JPEG mainly by using:
o: wavelets instead of the DCT
prediction instead of the DCT
a palette instead of full colour
larger blocks instead of 8 × 8
questions.hint: It has no blocking artifacts.
questions.r: Slide 54: JPEG 2000 uses wavelets, so there is no 8 × 8 blocking. JPEG-LS is the prediction-based one.

questions.q: JPEG AI is notable as the first JPEG standard that is:
o: built on end-to-end learned coding
able to restore JPEG files exactly
based on wavelets without blocks
limited to lossless compression
questions.hint: The name says it.
questions.r: Slide 54: JPEG AI is the first standard built on end-to-end learned coding. Exact JPEG recompression is JPEG XL; wavelets are JPEG 2000.

questions.q: LZW compresses data by:
o: building a dictionary of sequences as it reads
sending a full dictionary before the data
merging the two rarest symbols repeatedly
mapping the whole message to a single real number
questions.hint: The dictionary is not transmitted.
questions.r: Slide 55: LZW builds a dictionary of already seen sequences on the fly and emits short codes for them. Merging is Huffman; one number is arithmetic coding.

questions.q: Before DEFLATE, PNG applies to each row:
o: a prediction filter such as Sub, Up or Paeth
a cosine transform of eight neighbouring pixels
a subsampling step for the colour channels
a reduction to a palette of 256 colours
questions.hint: The same idea as lossless JPEG.
questions.r: Slide 55: PNG = prediction (row filters Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) + LZ77 + Huffman. It uses no DCT and no chroma subsampling.

questions.q: PNG stands for:
o: Portable Network Graphics
Progressive Network Graphics
Portable Network Gradients
Published Network Graphics
questions.hint: Made for the web.
questions.r: Slide 58: PNG = Portable Network Graphics, designed to replace GIF.

questions.q: Which type of redundancy does video coding remove that JPEG does not, giving the single largest gain?
o: Spatial redundancy
Statistical redundancy
Temporal redundancy
Perceptual redundancy
questions.hint: Think about what changes between one picture and the next, not inside one picture.
questions.r: Slide 6: JPEG already removes spatial, perceptual and statistical redundancy; video adds temporal (motion-compensated) prediction, the single largest gain. Spatial redundancy is handled by DCT/intra prediction, which JPEG already has.
questions.why: 'NEW IN VIDEO' tag + takeaway + summary slide 55

questions.q: Which pairing of redundancy type and the tool that removes it is CORRECT?
o: Statistical – chroma subsampling
Perceptual – quantization
Spatial – motion-compensated prediction
Temporal – CABAC entropy coding
questions.hint: Which tool throws away detail the eye would not notice anyway?
questions.r: Perceptual redundancy is removed by chroma subsampling and quantization (both lossy). Statistical goes with VLC/Huffman/CABAC, spatial with DCT/intra prediction, temporal with motion-compensated prediction.
questions.why: four-box table, repeated on summary slide 55

questions.q: Which set contains ONLY lossy steps of a video encoder?
o: Chroma subsampling and quantization
Quantization and CABAC
Huffman coding and chroma subsampling
VLC and CABAC
questions.hint: Lossy means information you can never get back. Entropy coding only gives symbols shorter names.
questions.r: Slide 9: chroma subsampling and quantization are both lossy. Slide 10: entropy coding (VLC/Huffman, CABAC) is lossless, so any set that contains it is wrong.
questions.why: 'LOSSY' tags on slides 6 and 9, 'Lossless' on slide 10

questions.q: Why is uncompressed UHD video impractical to send over a network?
o: Its raw data rate is far above a typical link
Its frames cannot be divided into small packets
Its colours need a special type of cable
Its frame rate is too low for streaming
questions.hint: Width × height × bits × frames adds up.
questions.r: Slide 5: raw UHD at 60 fps needs about 11.9 Gbit/s, roughly 12 times a 1 Gbit/s Ethernet link. Packets, cables and frame rate are not the obstacle.
questions.why: formula on slide 4 + big number box '11.9 Gbit/s'

questions.q: What is the raw data rate of 1920 × 1080, 10-bit, 4:2:0, 50 fps video?
o: ≈ 3.11 Gbit/s
≈ 2.07 Gbit/s
≈ 1.56 Gbit/s
≈ 1.04 Gbit/s
questions.hint: In 4:2:0 each pixel carries one luma sample plus two chroma samples at a quarter of the resolution each.
questions.r: 4:2:0 keeps 1 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1.5 samples per pixel, so 15 bit/pixel: 1920 × 1080 × 15 × 50 ≈ 1.56 Gbit/s. 3.11 Gbit/s would be 4:4:4 (30 bit/pixel) and 2.07 Gbit/s is 4:2:2 (20 bit/pixel).
questions.why: question 1 of the review slide "quiz on 27 November"

questions.q: PSNR measures quality by comparing:
o: the peak signal with the mean squared error, in dB
structure, contrast and luminance in local windows
the opinions of viewers on a scale from 1 to 5
several features combined by machine learning
questions.hint: Less error must give a HIGHER score. Where must MSE sit in the fraction?
questions.r: Slide 14: PSNR is the peak signal against the mean squared error, in decibels (about 30–45 dB for lossy video). The others describe SSIM, MOS and VMAF.
questions.why: formula box on slide 14

questions.q: Which pairing of quality metric and score range is correct according to the lecture?
o: PSNR: about 30-45 dB for typical lossy video
SSIM: 0-100, a learned fusion of features
VMAF: 1-5, collected from viewer tests
MOS: 0-1, computed in local windows
questions.hint: One metric is a logarithmic ratio of signal power to error; the others are bounded scores.
questions.r: Slide 14: PSNR is about 30-45 dB for lossy video; SSIM runs 0-1 (structure, contrast and luminance in local windows); VMAF 0-100 (Netflix's learned fusion); MOS 1-5 (viewer tests). Each distractor gives one metric another metric's range.
questions.why: three metric boxes with ranges side by side, easy to swap

questions.q: VMAF is:
o: A learned fusion of several features by Netflix (2016), scored 0–100
A structure, contrast and luminance index in local windows, range 0–1
A subjective Mean Opinion Score from viewer tests, on a 1–5 scale
A ratio of peak signal power to mean squared error, in dB
questions.hint: Which metric is the de-facto standard for streaming ladders, and which company streams video?
questions.r: Slide 14: VMAF (Netflix, 2016) fuses VIF, detail loss and a temporal motion feature; score 0–100; de-facto standard for streaming ladders. The other options describe SSIM, MOS and PSNR.
questions.why: sibling metric boxes on one slide, ideal for definition distractors

questions.q: A BD-rate of −40 % means that the tested codec needs:
o: 40 % less bit rate at the same quality
40 % more bit rate at the same quality
40 % less quality at the same bit rate
40 % less time for the same quality
questions.hint: BD-rate compares bit rates.
questions.r: Slide 15: BD-rate is the bit-rate difference at equal quality; a negative value is a saving.
questions.why: worked numeric example in the BD-rate box

questions.q: Which set contains ONLY codecs from the open / royalty-free line of the standards timeline?
o: VP9, AV1, EVC
VP8, AV1, AV2
AV1, LCEVC, VP8
questions.hint: Think AOMedia (Google, Netflix, Amazon, ...) and its predecessors: no H.26x, no MPEG standards.
questions.r: Slide 16: the open/royalty-free row holds VP8, VP9, AV1 and AV2. EVC and LCEVC are ISO/IEC MPEG standards; H.263 is an ITU-T VCEG standard.
questions.why: timeline grouped by standards body

questions.q: JVET, the joint group that developed VVC (H.266), stands for:
o: Joint Video Encoding Taskforce
Joint Visual Enhancement Team
Joint VCEG Engineering Team
Joint Video Experts Team
questions.hint: The joint teams went JVT → JCT-VC → JVET; the last one gathers the 'experts'.
questions.r: Slide 2: JVET = Joint Video Experts Team (VVC); JCT-VC = Joint Collaborative Team on Video Coding (HEVC). Since 2003 every main-line codec comes from these joint ITU-T / ISO-IEC teams.
questions.why: acronym list on slide 2, repeated in takeaway of slide 16

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT transmitted in the bitstream by a hybrid (MPEG-2-style) encoder?
o: Quantized DCT coefficients of the residual
The decoded reference frames from the frame buffer
Motion vectors and coding modes
Headers such as picture type and quantiser scale
questions.hint: The decoder rebuilds one of these itself by repeating the grey loop.
questions.r: Slide 18: only quantized residual coefficients, motion vectors/modes and headers are sent. The decoder rebuilds the reference frames itself by repeating the loop, nothing else.
questions.why: 'What is transmitted' box on the encoder diagram

questions.q: What is the correct MPEG-2 stream hierarchy, from the largest to the smallest unit?
o: Sequence → GOP → Picture → Slice → Macroblock → Block
Sequence → Picture → GOP → Macroblock → Slice → Block
GOP → Sequence → Picture → Slice → Block → Macroblock
Sequence → GOP → Slice → Picture → Block → Macroblock
questions.hint: A slice is a row of macroblocks inside one picture; the block is the 8×8 DCT unit.
questions.r: Slide 19: Sequence (whole video) → GOP (I-frame + dependants) → Picture → Slice (row of MBs) → Macroblock (16×16 luma) → Block (8×8 samples).
questions.why: six-box chain on slide 19, zoomed again on slide 20

questions.q: In MPEG-2, the macroblock is the unit of ___, and the 8×8 block is the unit of ___.
o: the DCT; motion
motion; the DCT
random access; the DCT
error resynchronization; motion
questions.hint: A motion vector moves a 16×16 luma area; the transform works on 8×8 samples.
questions.r: Slide 19: macroblock = 16×16 luma, unit of motion; block = 8×8 samples, unit of the DCT. Random access belongs to the GOP, and resynchronization after errors to the slice.
questions.why: each hierarchy box states its role

questions.q: How many 8×8 blocks make up one 4:2:0 macroblock in MPEG-2?
questions.hint: 16×16 luma gives four Y blocks; then add chroma at half resolution in both directions.
questions.r: Slide 19: 4 Y blocks + 1 Cb + 1 Cr = 6 blocks. With 4:2:2 the chroma doubles, giving 8 blocks.
questions.why: bold '4:2:0 macroblock = 6 blocks of 8 × 8'

questions.q: Which MPEG-2 frame type is usually compressed the most?
o: I-frames
P-frames
B-frames
I- and P-frames equally
questions.hint: It can look in two directions.
questions.r: Slide 21: B-frames use a previous and a next frame (about 50:1). P-frames use only a previous one (about 20:1) and I-frames none (about 10:1).
questions.why: three big numbers on slide 21, reused on slides 22, 37 and 56

questions.q: Which statement about B-frames in MPEG-2 is TRUE?
o: They are never used as a reference, so an error stays in one frame
They are predicted only from the previous I- or P-frame
They act as random-access points that stop error propagation
They give the least compression but need the least encoder work
questions.hint: Ask which other frames depend on a B-frame in MPEG-2.
questions.r: Slides 21 and 36: MPEG-2 B-frames are never a reference, so errors stay in one frame; they use the previous AND next anchor and give the most compression. Random access is the role of I-frames.
questions.why: stated on slides 21, 32 and 36

questions.q: What is the average compression of the GOP I B P B P B P B if I : P : B = 10 : 20 : 50?
questions.hint: Count the frame types first, then divide the number of frames by the sum of 1/ratio.
questions.r: 1 I, 3 P and 4 B: 8 / (1/10 + 3/20 + 4/50) = 8 / 0.33 ≈ 24:1 (method of slide 22). ≈ 34:1 comes from averaging the ratios; ≈ 29:1 is the 12-frame IBBP GOP of slide 22.
questions.why: question 3 of the review slide "quiz on 27 November"

questions.q: Display order: I1 B2 B3 P4 B5 B6 P7 ... The decoding / transmission order starts with:
o: I1 B2 B3 P4 B5 B6 P7
I1 P4 P7 B2 B3 B5 B6
I1 P4 B2 B3 P7 B5 B6
P4 I1 B2 B3 P7 B5 B6
questions.hint: A B-frame can be decoded only after BOTH of its anchors have arrived, and no earlier than needed.
questions.r: Slide 35: I1 P4 B2 B3 P7 B5 B6 P10 B8 B9 I13 B11 B12. Each anchor is sent just before the B-frames that need it; P4 must be decoded before B2 and B3.
questions.why: learning goal on slide 3 + slide 35 + review Q4

questions.q: In a container or PES stream, DTS and PTS mean:
o: DTS = when to decode a frame, PTS = when to show it
DTS = when to show a frame, PTS = when to decode it
DTS = data transport stream, PTS = picture type signal
DTS = decoder test sequence, PTS = program time slot
questions.hint: D for decoding, P for presentation. Both are needed because the two frame orders differ.
questions.r: Slide 35: decoding time stamp = when to decode, presentation time stamp = when to show; both live in the PES / container. They differ because B-frames are reordered.
questions.why: 'PTS and DTS' box on slide 35, again in container metadata on slide 51

questions.q: A closed GOP is one in which:
o: Leading B-frames use the previous GOP for slightly better efficiency
No prediction crosses the GOP border, allowing clean cuts and ABR segments
No B-frames are used, so the reordering delay is zero
Every P-frame refers back to the I-frame of the previous GOP
questions.hint: 'Closed' means the door to the neighbouring GOP is shut.
questions.r: Slide 36: closed GOP = no prediction across the GOP border, giving clean cuts, ad splicing and ABR segments. Leading B-frames that use the previous GOP describe an OPEN GOP.
questions.why: open vs closed contrast box; reused for ABR on slide 52

questions.q: According to the lecture, MPEG video standards define only:
o: The encoder and its motion search strategy
The matching criterion and the search window size
The bitstream and the decoder
The encoder, the decoder and the container
questions.hint: Encoders such as x264, x265 and hardware chips compete with each other. So what must be fixed?
questions.r: Slide 26 (highlighted): MPEG standards define only the bitstream and the decoder. The similarity criterion (usually SAD) and the search window ±p are 'not specified – the encoder decides'.
questions.why: yellow-highlighted key point

questions.q: For a search range of ±7, how many SAD evaluations does the three-step search (TSS) need compared with full search?
questions.hint: Step sizes 4, 2, 1: the first step tests 9 points, each later step adds 8 new points.
questions.r: Slide 29: TSS = 9 + 8 + 8 = 25 evaluations; full search over ±7 = 15 × 15 = 225 positions. The price is the risk of a local minimum instead of the best match.
questions.why: question 5 of the review slide "quiz on 27 November"

questions.q: Why is an MPEG-style codec called asymmetric?
o: Only the encoder does motion search; the decoder just copies the block the vector points to
The encoder uses the DCT while the decoder inverts it with a different wavelet transform
The decoder must repeat the full motion search, so it is more expensive
The upstream and downstream channels use different bit rates, like an ADSL internet link
questions.hint: Picture a broadcaster with one expensive encoder and millions of cheap TV sets.
questions.r: Slide 28: only the encoder pays for motion search (≈ 0.5·10^12 operations/s for full search on SD); the decoder only copies the referenced block. Hence cheap decoders in every TV and expensive encoders at the broadcaster.
questions.why: 'Only the encoder pays' box + slide 34 note + M-JPEG table on slide 12

questions.q: Why must the encoder predict from the DECODED reference frame rather than from the original frame?
o: The original frame is discarded by the encoder before motion estimation
Decoded frames contain less noise than originals, so the residual becomes zero and costs no bits
The standard forbids storing original frames in the encoder buffer, so only decoded ones remain
The decoder has only the decoded frame; otherwise both sides drift apart until the next I-frame
questions.hint: Encoder and decoder must predict from exactly the same picture.
questions.r: Slide 31 'Keep the loop closed': predicting from the original makes encoder and decoder drift apart, and the error accumulates until the next I-frame. That is why the encoder contains a decoder model (slide 18).
questions.why: red box on slide 31 + review question Q2

questions.q: Which pairing of rate-control mode and typical use is CORRECT?
o: CRF / CQ – broadcast multiplex (DVB)
CBR – broadcast multiplex (DVB)
2-pass VBR – live video calls
Capped CRF – archives of unknown size
questions.hint: A broadcast channel has a fixed capacity that must never overflow.
questions.r: Slide 38: CBR → broadcast multiplex (DVB); 2-pass VBR → disc, VOD; CRF/CQ → archives (size unknown in advance); capped CRF → streaming ladders.
questions.why: four rate-control boxes with use cases

questions.q: What does the FFmpeg option “-crf 23” (e.g. with libx264) select?
o: A constant bit rate of 23 Mbit/s with a buffer model
A two-pass VBR encode that analyses 23 frames before choosing bit rates
A GOP length of 23 frames between two consecutive I-frames in the stream
Constant-quality rate control; the file size is not known in advance
questions.hint: CRF = Constant Rate Factor: it targets quality, not size.
questions.r: Slide 38: CRF/CQ = constant quality (-crf); the file size is unknown in advance; used for archives. The GOP length is set with -g, not -crf. The lab task (slide 54) varies -crf 18 / 23 / 28 to trade file size against PSNR/VMAF.
questions.why: rate-control box + FFmpeg commands and lab task on slide 54

questions.q: From AVC to HEVC to VVC, the number of intra prediction modes:
o: grows with each generation
stays the same throughout
shrinks with each generation
is left to the encoder maker
questions.hint: Newer codecs have more tools, not fewer.
questions.r: Slide 40: 9 directions in AVC, 35 modes in HEVC and 67 in VVC.
questions.why: numbers on slide 23 and in the tool table on slide 40

questions.q: Compared with H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC offers approximately:
o: 50 % lower bit rate at ≈ 4× encoder complexity
30–50 % lower bit rate at several× encoder complexity
≈ 20 % lower bit rate at the same encoder complexity
40–50 % lower bit rate at up to ≈ 10× encoder complexity
questions.hint: The other figures belong to AVC vs MPEG-2, VVC vs HEVC and ECM vs VVC.
questions.r: Slide 45: HEVC ≈ 40–50 % lower bit rate than AVC at the same quality, encoder up to ≈ 10× (decoder ≈ 1.5–3×). 50 % / 4× is AVC vs MPEG-2 (slide 42); 30–50 % / several× is VVC vs HEVC (slide 46).
questions.why: big stat boxes on each codec slide, easy to cross-swap

questions.q: Each new main-line video codec generation roughly:
o: halves the bit rate at equal quality, with a more complex encoder
doubles the bit rate at equal quality, with a simpler encoder
keeps the bit rate and quality, with a much faster encoder
halves the bit rate and also halves the complexity of the encoder
questions.hint: Better compression has a price.
questions.r: Slide 48: the bit rate for equal quality roughly halves about every ten years, while the encoder becomes 2 to 10 times more complex.
questions.why: bar chart 'codec generations at a glance' + summary 'each generation saves 30–50 %'

questions.q: Which statement about a container such as MP4 (ISO BMFF) is TRUE?
o: It compresses the video track itself, with its own transform and quantizer
It multiplexes and time-stamps tracks; the extension names no codec
It always carries H.264 video with AAC audio, as the .mp4 extension implies
It sets the motion-vector precision and the GOP structure of the video
questions.hint: Codec ≠ container: one packs, the other compresses.
questions.r: Slide 51: a container multiplexes and time-stamps (video, audio, subtitle tracks, metadata with PTS/DTS); the codec compresses. '.mp4' says nothing about the codec inside; check with ffprobe.
questions.why: 'Remember' takeaway on slide 51

questions.q: In adaptive bit-rate streaming (HLS, MPEG-DASH), each 2–6 s segment starts with:
o: An IDR picture
A bi-directional B-frame
A predicted P-frame
A skipped macroblock row
questions.hint: The player must be able to start decoding any segment of any rendition on its own.
questions.r: Slide 52: segments of 2–6 s each start with an IDR, and renditions use aligned, closed GOPs for seamless switching. An IDR also empties the reference buffer (slide 36).
questions.why: heading 'Segments of 2 - 6 s, each starting with an IDR'

questions.q: Which HDR transfer function is backward compatible and intended for broadcast?
o: PQ (SMPTE ST 2084)
Gamma (BT.1886)
HLG
questions.hint: The other HDR curve reaches 10 000 cd/m² but is not the backward-compatible one.
questions.r: Slide 53: HLG is backward compatible, for broadcast. PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) goes up to 10 000 cd/m²; BT.1886 gamma is SDR; BT.2020 is a colour gamut, not a transfer function.
questions.why: transfer function box with three sibling items

questions.q: How do HDR10 and HDR10+ / Dolby Vision differ in their metadata?
o: HDR10 is static, one value per film; HDR10+ / Dolby Vision are dynamic, per scene
HDR10 is dynamic, per scene; HDR10+ / Dolby Vision are static, one value per film
HDR10 uses 8-bit metadata; HDR10+ / Dolby Vision use 10-bit metadata
HDR10 requires HLG; HDR10+ / Dolby Vision require PQ only for broadcast
questions.hint: The '+' version added something that can change during the film.
questions.r: Slide 53: HDR10 = static metadata, one value per film; HDR10+ and Dolby Vision = dynamic metadata, per scene.
questions.why: metadata box contrasting static and dynamic

questions.q: Spatial redundancy means that:
o: neighbouring pixels are similar
consecutive frames are similar
some symbols are more frequent than others
the eye misses fine detail
questions.hint: Space, not time.
questions.r: Slide 6: spatial = neighbouring pixels, temporal = consecutive frames, statistical = symbol frequencies, perceptual = what the eye misses.

questions.q: A GOP (group of pictures) is:
o: an I-frame and the frames depending on it
a group of macroblocks with one motion vector
all the B-frames that lie between two P-frames
a set of tracks stored in the same container
questions.hint: It is the unit of random access.
questions.r: Slide 19: GOP = I-frame + its dependants; decoding can start at its I-frame.

questions.q: An I-frame is:
o: coded using only its own pixels
predicted from the previous anchor
predicted from two other frames
copied from the previous frame
questions.hint: I stands for intra.
questions.r: Slide 21: an I-frame uses only its own pixels (JPEG-like), is a random-access point and stops error propagation.

questions.q: In MPEG-2, a P-frame is predicted from:
o: the last I- or P-frame
the next I- or P-frame
the previous two B-frames
the previous and next frame
questions.hint: It looks in one direction only.
questions.r: Slide 21: P = predicted from the previous I or P frame. B-frames use the previous and the next anchor and are never references in MPEG-2.

questions.q: In motion search, SAD stands for:
o: Sum of Absolute Differences
Search Area Distance
Sample Adaptive Distortion Value
Sum of Averaged Deltas
questions.hint: It measures how similar two blocks are.
questions.r: Slide 26: the usual matching criterion is the Sum of Absolute Differences. The standard leaves the choice to the encoder.

questions.q: A motion vector tells the decoder:
o: which block of the reference frame to copy
how fast the camera was moving during the shot
which frames to skip on a slow network
how many bits the next macroblock may use
questions.hint: The decoder does not search.
questions.r: Slide 28: the decoder just copies the block the vector points to; only the encoder searches.

questions.q: In a P-frame, the residual is:
o: the difference between a block and its prediction
the distance between a block and its nearest match
the part of a frame outside the search window
the space left in the encoder output buffer
questions.hint: What prediction did not get right.
questions.r: Slide 31: after motion compensation the encoder codes the residual (block minus prediction) with DCT, quantization and VLC. The distance to the match is the motion vector.

questions.q: Compared with a short GOP, a long GOP gives:
o: better compression, slower seeking
worse compression, but faster seeking
better compression and faster seeking
equal compression but more I-frames
questions.hint: Fewer I-frames.
questions.r: Slide 36: long GOP = fewer I-frames, better compression; short GOP = faster channel change, seeking and error recovery.

questions.q: In adaptive bit-rate streaming, the player:
o: picks the next segment to match its throughput
asks the server to encode the video again
drops all the B-frames when the network is slow
downloads all versions and shows the best
questions.hint: It changes rung on the ladder.
questions.r: Slide 52: the client measures throughput and buffer and picks the next segment from the ladder of renditions.

questions.q: Why is AVC the safe choice for live streaming to any device?
o: Nearly every device decodes it
It needs the lowest bit rate of all
It is completely free of licence fees
It was designed for UHD and HDR video
questions.hint: Support matters as much as efficiency.
questions.r: Question 6 of the review slide (56). AVC is decoded almost everywhere and is cheap to encode live. For a large VOD library HEVC or AV1 pay off: each title is encoded once and streamed many times, so the saved bit rate outweighs the encoding cost (AV1 is royalty-free). Slide 48: adoption depends on licensing and hardware support as much as on efficiency.
